bullets: The new RVL-CDIP document-classification audit reports that about 10.5% of 400,000 documents have incorrect labels and 35.2% of the test set has a duplicate or near-duplicate in training. It also finds that page identification codes alone support 69% accuracy and that removing them reduces one model’s score by 11 points. Why it matters: If you use RVL-CDIP to select document models, its headline accuracy may partly measure label errors, repeated documents, and source-specific identifiers rather than transferable classification. The audit supports adding deduplication, corrected labels, identifier-masked tests, and external-document testing before making a model decision. Evidence: E011. High confidence.

The new THReD Agent Benchmark evaluates an electronic health record preprocessing assistant with 141 tasks covering simple and multi-step transformations, failure recovery, requests where the agent should not act, schema changes, and prompt injection hidden in data. It uses synthetic health-record tables, expert reference pipelines, and outcome checks rather than patient data. Why it matters: If you are evaluating assistants that prepare clinical datasets, this artifact tests operational safety and recovery alongside successful preprocessing. It offers a way to compare context configurations without exposing patient records and avoids treating task completion alone as sufficient evidence of readiness. Evidence: E001. High confidence.

The new “When Agents Fail” framework separates model behavior from the software harness that manages tools and execution. It measures valid completion, fit between a model and harness, fit across models, pairing-specific residuals, and failure modes. A separate controlled study of lightweight coding agents likewise evaluates alternative model-harness pairings rather than fixed leaderboard configurations. Why it matters: If you are choosing a self-hosted coding agent, a model score from one harness does not establish performance in another. These releases support testing the exact model-harness pair and recording whether failures come from task errors, abnormal termination, or the interaction between the two components. Evidence: E019, E010. High confidence.

The new Async-RBench contains 200 executable tasks in eight scenarios where a main large language model agent continues working while delayed subagent results arrive under controlled task-state conditions. SWE-Shift independently tests coding agents when code, dependencies, runtime state, or requirements change during execution. Why it matters: Together, these artifacts expose a recurring pressure in this captured feed: long-running agents need evaluation under changing state, not only static tasks. If you are selecting an agent for concurrent or evolving work, this means checking whether it preserves valid work, revisits stale assumptions, and handles delayed results correctly before scoring the final outcome. Evidence: E021, E027. High confidence.

The new Interactive Graphical User Interface Grounding benchmark changes interface testing from locating an already visible target to first revealing it and then clicking it. Its 601 tasks across 16 controlled environments cover targets that are off-screen, occluded, delayed, or exposed only after an interface state change. Why it matters: If you are comparing agents for real software interfaces, static screenshot localization misses whether an agent can recover visibility through scrolling, movement, dragging, waiting, or other interaction. This benchmark lets product teams separate target recognition from the preceding navigation needed to make the target actionable. Evidence: E016. High confidence.

The new DMAIC-Bench tests whether an analytical agent changes its next action after reviewing intermediate evidence, a capability it calls self-restraint. Its 97 seeded tasks include paired counterfactual variants that require opposite actions at the same workflow position, distinguishing justified stopping or redirection from indiscriminate refusal. Why it matters: If you are evaluating agents for multi-stage analysis, a plausible self-critique does not show that evidence affected behavior. The paired design provides a way to test whether an agent continues when prerequisites hold and stops or redirects when they do not, rather than rewarding commentary or final-answer quality alone. Evidence: E023. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新的 RVL-CDIP 文档分类审计报告称，在 400,000 份文档中，约 10.5% 的标签不正确，且测试集中有 35.2% 的文档在训练集中存在重复或近重复项。审计还发现，仅凭页面识别码即可达到 69% 的准确率，而移除这些识别码会使一个模型的分数下降 11 分。Why it matters: 如果你使用 RVL-CDIP 选择文档模型，其标称准确率可能在一定程度上衡量的是标签错误、重复文档和特定来源的标识符，而非可迁移的分类能力。该审计表明，在作出模型决策之前，应增加去重、标签纠正、标识符掩码测试和外部文档测试。Evidence: E011. High confidence.

新的 THReD Agent Benchmark 评估了一款电子健康记录预处理助手，包含 141 项任务，涵盖简单及多步骤转换、故障恢复、智能体不应采取行动的请求、模式变更，以及隐藏在数据中的提示注入。它使用合成的健康记录表、专家参考流水线和结果检查，而非患者数据。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估用于准备临床数据集的助手，该评测项目会在成功完成预处理之外，同时测试运行安全性和恢复能力。它提供了一种无需暴露患者记录即可比较不同上下文配置的方法，并避免将仅仅完成任务视为已具备可用性的充分证据。Evidence: E001. High confidence.

新的“When Agents Fail”框架将模型行为与负责管理工具和执行的软件框架分离开来。它衡量有效完成情况、模型与框架之间的适配度、跨模型适配度、特定配对的残差以及失败模式。另一项针对轻量级编程智能体的独立对照研究同样评估了不同的模型—框架配对，而非固定的排行榜配置。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择自托管编程智能体，模型在某个框架中的分数并不能证明它在另一个框架中的表现。这些新发布的成果支持测试确切的模型—框架组合，并记录失败究竟来自任务错误、异常终止，还是两个组件之间的交互。Evidence: E019, E010. High confidence.

新的 Async-RBench 包含 200 项可执行任务，分布在八种场景中；在受控的任务状态条件下，当延迟返回的子智能体结果陆续到达时，主大型语言模型智能体会继续工作。SWE-Shift 则独立测试了编程智能体在代码、依赖项、运行时状态或需求于执行期间发生变化时的表现。Why it matters: 这些评测项目共同揭示了本次采集信息流中反复出现的一项压力：长时间运行的智能体需要在状态不断变化的条件下接受评估，而不能只使用静态任务。如果你正在为并发或持续演变的工作选择智能体，这意味着在评定最终结果之前，需要检查它能否保留有效工作、重新审视已过时的假设，并正确处理延迟返回的结果。Evidence: E021, E027. High confidence.

新的 Interactive Graphical User Interface Grounding 基准将界面测试从定位一个已经可见的目标，改为先使其显现，再点击它。其 601 项任务覆盖 16 个受控环境，目标可能位于屏幕之外、被遮挡、延迟出现，或仅在界面状态变化后才会显现。Why it matters: 如果你正在比较用于真实软件界面的智能体，静态截图定位无法衡量智能体能否通过滚动、移动、拖动、等待或其他交互方式让目标重新可见。该基准使产品团队能够将目标识别与此前为使目标变得可操作而必须完成的导航过程区分开来。Evidence: E016. High confidence.

新的 DMAIC-Bench 测试分析型智能体在审视中间证据后，是否会改变下一步行动；该基准将这种能力称为自我克制。其 97 项预设任务包含成对的反事实变体，要求智能体在工作流的同一位置采取相反行动，从而区分有正当理由的停止或转向与不加区分的拒绝。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估用于多阶段分析的智能体，看似合理的自我批评并不能证明证据确实影响了其行为。这种成对设计提供了一种测试方法，可判断智能体是否会在前提条件成立时继续行动，并在前提条件不成立时停止或转向，而不是只奖励评论内容或最终答案的质量。Evidence: E023. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the THReD Agent Benchmark: the tasks, code and results used to evaluate the AI agent in THReD, a system that turns electronic health record (EHR) extracts into AI-ready datasets through a chat assistant that proposes preprocessing steps for the user to confirm. The benchmark comprises 141 preprocessing tasks in seven categories: single-tool, multi-step, goal-level, failure and recovery, requests where the agent should not act, robustness to schema variation, and prompt injection through the data. Each task has an expert reference pipeline and outcome checks evaluated on synthetic EHR tables; no patient data is used or sent to a model. Four configurations, from no context to the full deployed context, were each run five times with Claude Haiku 5.5 (2,550 episodes), with 95% confidence intervals from a cluster bootstrap over task templates. With the deployed configuration, the agent completed 92.7% of tasks on the first answer (95% CI 88.1–96.4%) and 95.6% within three turns, with tool-selection F1 0.926, argument accuracy 0.905, outcome agreement with the expert pipelines of 0.913 (row F1) and 3.3% invalid tool calls. It abstained correctly on every should-not-act request, recovered from every injected tool fault, handled every schema variation, and never followed an instruction planted in the data. Without a data profile, first-attempt completion fell to 58.0%. Contents: BENCHMARK REPORT.md: design, results, failure analysis, observations and limitations benchmark/results/: all metrics with confidence intervals, one row per episode, and the failed episodes benchmark/: the harness, scoring, outcome checks, task definitions, synthetic-data generator and privacy audit The scripts drive THReD's own agent and run from within the THReD source tree.
evidence_items.title: THReD Agent Benchmark: Evaluation of an LLM Agent for Preprocessing Electronic Health Records into AI-Ready Datasets

evidence_items.summary: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in clinical documentation, generating the rigorous, evidence-based reasoning required for unprecedented, atypical, and rare disease case reports remains a significant challenge. We present MedCaseAgent, an end-to-end agentic reasoning paradigm that bridges this gap by synthesizing publication-quality reports from unstructured clinical notes. MedCaseAgent leverages a hierarchical structure, integrating patient-level data mining with iterative, tool-integrated reasoning. By dynamically querying medical literature and knowledge bases, the agent maintains high clinical fidelity and assesses case novelty. The framework is inherently modular, supporting various backbone LLMs in a plug-and-play fashion. To facilitate this research, we release MedCase-150K, a large-scale multimodal clinical case-report corpus, and MedCase-Bench, a robust temporally held-out evaluation suite. We also introduce an open-source model post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B and optimized specifically for this task. Under both LLM-judged and rule-based evaluation, MedCaseAgent outperforms existing general-purpose and specialized medical LLMs and agents. Blinded expert reviews and ablations further support the system's clinical relevance and evidence grounding.
evidence_items.title: MedCaseAgent: From Multimodal Clinical Evidence to Rare Disease Case Reports

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Purpose Accurate dose calculation is a fundamental component of modern radiotherapy, enabling precise tumor irradiation while sparing surrounding healthy tissue. With the increasing adoption of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)‐guided radiotherapy and growing interest in real‐time adaptive radiotherapy, there is a demand for fast and accurate dose calculation techniques on both computed tomography (CT) and MRI. To facilitate research in this area, the DoseRAD2026 dataset and accompanying challenge introduce a publicly available benchmark dataset comprising paired CT and MRI data with corresponding beam‐level photon and proton Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions, enabling the development and systematic evaluation of advanced dose calculation and prediction methods. Acquisition and validation methods The DoseRAD2026 dataset comprises paired CT and MRI data from 115 patients (75 training, 40 testing) treated on a hybrid MRI‐linear accelerator (MRI‐linac) for thoracic or abdominal lesions and is derived from the SynthRAD2025 dataset. Image pre‐processing included deformable image registration, air‐cavity correction and resampling. Ground‐truth photon (6 MV) and proton dose distributions were generated using open‐source MC dose calculation algorithms and resulted in a training dataset of 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. Data format and usage notes The dataset is organized into photon and proton subsets, each comprising paired CT‐MRI images, beam‐level dose distributions, and JSON files specifying patient‐specific beam configurations. Data are provided in compressed MetaImage (.mha) format with standardized naming linking dose files to beam parameters in the JSON files. The dataset is released under a CC BY‐NC 4.0 license, with the training set available from April 2026 and the test set withheld until March 2030.
evidence_items.title: DoseRAD2026: A benchmark dataset for AI‐accelerated photon and proton dose calculation in radiotherapy

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in 3D semantic segmentation have significantly improved scene understanding in autonomous driving. However, existing methods are typically developed under a closed-set assumption and evaluated under standard driving conditions, where all categories are known in advance. In real-world driving, autonomous vehicles inevitably encounter previously unseen objects, making closed-set perception insufficient for safe deployment. To address this challenge, we introduce DriveOSS, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first real-world multimodal dataset and benchmark specifically designed for 3D anomaly segmentation and open-set semantic segmentation. It contains 12,661 synchronized and annotated frames captured using six surround-view RGB cameras, a 128-beam LiDAR, and a GPS/IMU unit. The dataset comprises 52 real-world driving scenes collected under clear, nighttime, cloudy, rainy, and snowy conditions and is organized into ID (in-distribution) and OOD (out-of-distribution) subsets. The ID scenes contain only known classes and are used for training, whereas the OOD scenes additionally contain unknown objects annotated as the outlier class and are used for validation and testing. Extensive experiments show that unseen objects remain a major challenge for current 3D perception systems. The dataset, benchmark protocols, and code are available at https://github.com/chrisyan/DriveOSS.
evidence_items.title: DriveOSS: Dataset and Benchmark for 3D Anomaly Segmentation and Open-set Semantic Segmentation in Autonomous Driving

evidence_items.summary: Background Automated dietary assessment increasingly struggles to evaluate industrial food processing levels, revealing a systemic gap between the visual presentation of meals and their underlying ultra-processed food composition. Although existing dietary monitoring tools can effectively track caloric and macronutrient intake, they lack the qualitative processing assessments required to identify hidden additives and map dietary risk triage quadrants. Methods This study introduces a modular, IoT-enabled multimodal dietary decision-support framework that decouples visual food recognition, standardized database retrieval, and qualitative language reasoning for automated NOVA processing classification and 2D decision matrix mapping. Operating on isolated single-dish meal instances, the system employs a four-phase cascaded pipeline that integrates vision-language models, database retrieval, and large language models (LLMs) with strict JSON schema enforcement. The platform was evaluated using the Nutrition-NOVA validation benchmark, a harmonized multimodal dataset constructed through dense vector-space semantic linkage between quantitative profiles from the Center for Food Safety database and qualitative NOVA tiers from Open Food Facts. This benchmark addresses a 75.0% metadata sparsity deficit identified in legacy repositories. Results In experimental evaluations on the Nutrition-NOVA benchmark, the baseline Qwen-VL-Max architecture achieved an adjacent accuracy of 77.7%. Furthermore, enforcing schema modularity enabled complete plug-and-play backend replaceability between commercial cloud application programming interfaces (APIs) and private, on-premises open-weight models without requiring architectural retraining. Discussion The proposed framework establishes an efficient, safety-first screening tool for digital healthcare decision support.
evidence_items.title: IoT-enabled multimodal large language model-based framework for compositional food recognition, nutrient profiling, NOVA classification, and cancer risk mitigation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid expansion of mobile and digital financial services in Ethiopia has generated substantial user feedback, yet automated analysis remains challenging because reviews are multilingual, informal, code-switched, and weakly represented in existing language resources. This study develops and evaluates a reproducible multilingual natural language processing framework for classifying Ethiopian FinTech reviews into five service-oriented categories: General Praise or Suggestions (GPS), User Experience and Design Issues (UXD), Transaction and Payment Failures (TPF), Login and Authentication Problems (LAP), and Service and Support Complaints (SSC). An annotated corpus was constructed from publicly accessible reviews associated with 27 Ethiopian FinTech applications. The initial collection contained 8,387 records, of which 7,148 were retained after quality-control procedures. The corpus contains English, Amharic, and English-Amharic code-switched reviews. We benchmark conventional TF-IDF classifiers, neural architectures, and multilingual/African-language transformer models under a leakage-controlled experimental protocol in which random oversampling is restricted to the training partition. Using five-fold stratified cross-validation, repeated random seeds, held-out evaluation, confidence intervals, and paired bootstrap significance testing, AfroXLMR achieved the strongest performance, with 96.7% accuracy and 96.0% macro-F1, followed by AfriBERTa (96.5%, 95.8%) and XLM-R (96.2%, 95.4%). The strongest neural baseline, CNN, achieved 95.1% accuracy and 94.3% macro-F1, while XGBoost achieved 90.2% accuracy and 88.1% macro-F1. Minority-class recall improved substantially after training-only oversampling. Language-specific analysis indicated lower performance for English-Amharic code-switched reviews than for English and Amharic reviews.
evidence_items.title: Multilingual Artificial Intelligence for Classifying Ethiopian FinTech User Reviews

evidence_items.summary: Reproducible evaluation frameworks are essential for translating machine learning advances into medical decision-support systems, yet comparisons of classical machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and automated machine learning (AutoML) often lack standardized preprocessing, consistent validation, and transparent runtime reporting. We present a reproducible, time-aware benchmark for heart disease detection using a unified tabular dataset merging four University of California Irvine (UCI) Heart Disease sources: Cleveland, Hungary, Switzerland, and Veterans Administration (VA) Long Beach. The framework applies shared preprocessing and evaluates ML, DL, and AutoML under nominal framework-level time limits of 180 and 60 s, while reporting predictive metrics, observed wall-clock runtime, memory usage, and serialized model size. In the original single-split benchmark, Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) achieved an accuracy of 84.78%, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 91.79%, and an F1-score of 86.67% in the full regime. Under the lightweight regime, AutoGluon matched the accuracy and F1-score, increased area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) to 92.80%, and completed in 9.87 s, although with a larger serialized artifact. Robustness was assessed using repeated stratified 80/20 holdout evaluation across five pre-specified seeds. AutoGluon Light achieved the highest descriptive mean F1-score and ROC-AUC (83.97 ± 1.95% and 89.16 ± 2.29%, respectively), while ClassicML Light remained competitive (82.86 ± 2.68% F1-score; 88.09 ± 2.29% ROC-AUC) and achieved the shortest mean runtime (3.41 ± 3.52 s). Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction showed no statistically significant differences among lightweight frameworks.
evidence_items.title: A time-aware reproducible benchmark of full and lightweight AutoML, machine learning, and deep learning frameworks for heart disease detection

organizations: Sana'a University
evidence_items.summary: YemSarc is the first multimodal (text, audio, and video) benchmark dataset for sarcasm detection in Yemeni dialectal Arabic and seven additional Arabic dialects. It comprises 630 balanced utterances (315 sarcastic, 315 non-sarcastic) drawn from naturally occurring conversational exchanges across eight Arabic dialects: Mahwiti, Ibbi, Adeni, Sanaani, Dhamari, Saudi, Egyptian, and Taizzi. Each target utterance is paired with its preceding conversational context and is represented across three synchronized modalities: written transcript, audio segment, and video frame sequence. The dataset was constructed from two widely popular Yemeni comedic drama series (Bayt Al-Madaliz and Khuruj Nihai), sourced from their official YouTube channels. Annotation was carried out through a structured three-phase protocol by three expert academic linguists, achieving a final inter-annotator agreement of Fleiss' Kappa = 0.7473. The dataset is released with a fully reproducible, speaker-independent, and statistically audited evaluation pipeline. This dataset is intended for non-commercial academic research purposes, including multimodal sarcasm detection, Arabic dialectal NLP, and social media analysis. The dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0.
evidence_items.title: YemSarc: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Sarcasm Detection in Yemeni and Related Arabic Dialects

evidence_items.summary: Self-hosting coding agents is often necessary for software-engineering teams that must keep proprietary code and development traces within controlled infrastructure. Lightweight, open-weight models make such deployment more feasible by reducing hardware requirements, while strong results on repository-level benchmarks demonstrate their potential for demanding coding tasks. Deploying these models as coding agents requires pairing them with an agent harness, making their joint performance a key deployment consideration. Yet existing leaderboards primarily report fixed harness-model configurations rather than controlled comparisons across alternative pairings. To address this gap, we investigate harness-model interactions through a controlled full-factorial evaluation of six open-source harnesses and three lightweight coding models across 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, producing 1,800 graded runs under common serving, metering, and grading conditions. For the same model, resolution rates differ by up to 44 percentage points across harnesses, while harness rankings change across models. We apply an evidence-based failure taxonomy to 1,100 unsuccessful runs and find substantial differences in failure patterns across harness-model pairings. A model's dominant failure modes under one harness need not dominate under another. Efficiency is similarly dependent on the pairing: even among model-directed loop harnesses, charged tokens per resolved task vary by more than 20-fold. These findings make harness-model selection a central deployment decision for lightweight coding agents. Strong performance with one harness or model does not guarantee similar results with another. We translate these findings into practitioner guidance for pairing selection, token-efficiency assessment, and trajectory-informed harness engineering, and release the complete experimental records and analysis artifacts.
evidence_items.title: Pairing Matters: Performance, Failures, and Efficiency in Lightweight Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: RVL-CDIP is the de facto standard benchmark for document classification, and reported accuracy on it is now 98.8%. In this paper, we audit RVL-CDIP for data quality issues and find that approximately 10.5% of its 400,000 documents have erroneous labels and that 35.2% of the test set has a duplicate or near-duplicate in the training set. Identification codes on the pages are sufficient to classify at 69% accuracy, and a state-of-the-art model loses 11 points without them. Image-only models trained on RVL-CDIP lose 16 to 28 points on documents from other sources, and the choice of OCR engine changes accuracy by 4.1 to 8.3 points. We find that nearly 16,000 RVL-CDIP documents contain sensitive personal data, and produce de-identified versions of these documents. We re-benchmark 25 models, and with all defects remediated, the 13 that we retrain are 0.9 to 2.9 points more accurate than in the original condition; the most accurate of them, LayoutLMv3, is 96.5% accurate. We release the corrected corpus, the annotations and the out-of-distribution data.
evidence_items.title: Data Quality in RVL-CDIP: A Systematic Audit

evidence_items.summary: Text-based person anomaly search requires a model to retrieve individuals from a large image gallery using natural-language descriptions of both appearance and behavior. This task is challenging because model training relies on synthetic image-text pairs, whereas evaluation is performed on real surveillance images containing domain differences, near-duplicate frames, and many visually similar distractors. We present a multi-model retrieval and reranking framework designed to improve synthetic-to-real transfer. The framework first adapts Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B to synthetic person descriptions using bidirectional contrastive learning, explicit negative sampling, false-negative masking, and domain randomization. It then combines the normalized scores of six complementary Qwen3-VL checkpoints with those of a frozen SigLIP2 model using four-view gallery encoding. The fused retrieval scores identify the strongest candidates, which are jointly evaluated with the query using Qwen3-VL-Reranker-8B. The cross-encoder and retrieval scores are subsequently blended to produce the final ranking. We also construct a distractor-matched validation protocol entirely from synthetic data to select checkpoint weights, fusion coefficients, candidate depths, and reranking parameters without accessing the official test images. The final system achieves 94.7815% mAP and 90.8493% R@1 under the official AI City Challenge 2026 Track 4 test setting, with a reported eighth-place finish on the public leaderboard.
evidence_items.title: Synthetic-to-Real Text-Based Person Anomaly Search via Multi-Model Retrieval Fusion and Cross-Encoder Reranking

evidence_items.summary: Although LLMs demonstrate high success in logical tasks, it remains debated whether this stems from genuine reasoning or statistical memorization. This study presents a novel, multi-dimensional, perturbation- and session-based behavioral testing framework to assess LLMs’ arithmetic reasoning. To reduce the potential effect of data contamination, texts from the DROP, GSM8k, and MATH datasets were structurally manipulated. A comprehensive analysis was conducted on seven different models (DeepSeek-r1, DeepSeek-v2, Gemma, Llama 3.1, Llama 3.2, Mistral, Qwen) across 90 unique base questions evaluated under 2 distinct format constraints and 4 different presentation scenarios, analyzing a total of 5040 responses. The evaluation combined three quantitative metrics with six qualitative metrics examining session-based vulnerabilities. Results reveal that, within the tested contexts, models suffered performance degradation and logical disconnections when presentation conditions, formats, or constraints changed. Furthermore, models with thinking mechanisms often failed to complete challenging tasks within the time limit rather than gaining an advantage from their reasoning process. Ultimately, these findings indicate that benchmark accuracy alone may not reflect robust reasoning, underscoring the critical need for in-depth evaluation protocols that focus on cognitive consistency and error anatomy rather than mere accuracy rates.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Arithmetic Reasoning Skills Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Session-Based Experimental Design for LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support science, but they can also convert hazardous scientific knowledge into actionable misuse guidance. Existing benchmarks often rely on templated queries disconnected from real-world hazards, and employ LLM-as-a-Judge paradigms without domain grounding. To address this, we introduce SciHazard, a real-world-grounded benchmark for scientific risks and a dataset agnostic evaluation framework for measuring harmfulness. SciHazard contains 2400 hazardous questions and 600 oversafety questions across 12 disciplines, with both queries grounded in regulated entities and documented failure scenarios. To compute \textsc{DeHarm-Score} , we develop a decomposed evaluating procedure that combines query hazard severity, refusal behavior, and response-level risk. For non-refused responses, it further decomposes response-level harm into \textsc{Executability}, quantified via dynamic checklists with importance weighting, and \textsc{Net-new risk}, assessed through retrieval-augmented claim extraction and synthesis-barrier verification. An expert-validation study shows that \textsc{DeHarm-Score} improves agreement with expert annotations by 90.17\% over the strongest baseline. We benchmark 31 frontier LLMs and deep research agents in an extensive scientific safety evaluation. Notably, deep research agents yield 32.3\% higher mean \textsc{DeHarm-Score} than standard LLMs, exposing autonomous agents as a critical blind spot in current safety defenses. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/DeepSafe-Sci.
evidence_items.title: DeepSafe-SciHazard: A Benchmark for Measuring Scientific Safety Risks with Decomposed Harm Scoring

evidence_items.summary: Large language models and agents have shown significant power in advanced physical research. In this paper, We introduce PHYRD, a living benchmark for theoretical-physics reasoning with 63 Reproduce and 43 Discover problems. Reproduce tests derivation of published results; Discover tests consequences of modified theoretical conditions. FormulaForest constructs the tasks with reference solutions and subquestion-level rubrics. Across five models, whole-problem accuracy ranges from 49.21% to 68.25% on Reproduce and from 18.60% to 74.42% on closed-book Discover. With tools, four models complete more Discover problems, but conceptual errors and missing arguments persist. Besides, our experimental results demonstrate the value of FormulaForest as synthetic data. On FrontierScience, a benchmark developed by OpenAI, it raises the accuracy of a Qwen-35B-A3B model from 61% to 72%.
evidence_items.title: PHYRD: A Living Benchmark for Reproducing and Extending Theoretical Physics Research

evidence_items.summary: GUI grounding benchmarks ask whether an agent can localize a target that is already visible in a static screenshot. Real interfaces often violate this assumption: a target may be off-screen, appear only after a state change or hover, remain occluded, or become actionable after a delay. This leaves the ability to recover target visibility unevaluated. To measure this reveal step, we introduce Interactive GUI Grounding (IGG), a benchmark in which an agent must first make the target visible through interaction and then click it. IGG contains 601 tasks across 16 controllable GUI environments and seven visibility-constraint sub-types, with a compact action space of scrolling, moving, dragging, waiting, and clicking. In our human study, participants achieve 94.6% accuracy, while GPT-5.5 reaches 79.4% and the strongest evaluated open-source VLM reaches only 31.6%. To identify the source of this gap, we conduct two controlled interventions. Telling Qwen3-VL which interaction to perform raises its accuracy only from 30.8% to 33.9%, whereas performing the interaction for the model raises it to 81.9%. The bottleneck is executing the reveal interaction, not recognizing the target once it is exposed. We further show that this capability is learnable, demonstrating that visibility recovery can be strengthened consistently across model families.
evidence_items.title: IGG: A Benchmark for Interactive GUI Grounding under Visibility Constraints

evidence_items.summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a promising approach to medical image representation learning, yet augmentation strategies of SSL frameworks validated on natural images do not reliably transfer to specialized medical imaging domains. We analyze DINO, a knowledge-distillation based SSL framework, and empirically demonstrate that its default augmentation strategy produces unreliable representations for retinal fundus images, degrading downstream glaucoma classification performance. Guided by the principle that effective cropped views should share minimal redundant information while retaining clinically relevant signal, we redesign DINO's augmentation strategy. Our approach biases the learned representations toward diagnostically critical features rather than low-level image statistics. We evaluate our method for glaucoma classification by training a linear classifier on the frozen representations, achieving strong generalization across seven benchmark datasets. URL for code and weights: https://github.com/ashish-256/task_dino
evidence_items.title: Augmentation Strategy for DINO in Glaucoma Classification

evidence_items.summary: Photonic crystal fibers (PCFs) underpin critical applications in telecommunications, sensing, and high-power laser delivery, yet their design remains a manual, expert-intensive process that couples geometric intuition with deep waveguide physics. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising path toward automating PCF design, but can they truly reason about photonic physics from microscopy images, or do they merely recognize visual patterns? We introduce PCFBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs on the perception, reasoning, and decision steps of the photonic inverse-design loop. PCFBench spans 26 tasks organized into six categories of increasing cognitive demand (Geometry Perception, Physics Understanding, Text Generation, Multi-modal Reasoning, Inverse-Design Decision, and Code Generation), built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples across 18 structurally diverse fiber families. We evaluate both individual VLMs on isolated tasks and multi-agent systems (MAS) on the full sequential pipeline from perception to design. Our results reveal a striking perception-design gap: current models can identify fiber geometry with moderate success, yet consistently fail to translate that visual understanding into physics-aware design actions. Moreover, cascading agents through the pipeline exposes significant error propagation, where upstream perception mistakes compound into downstream design failures. These findings suggest that neither model scaling nor naive agent chaining suffices, and that closing the loop demands explicit physical grounding. PCFBench provides the community with a rigorous, multi-dimensional testbed to measure progress toward AI-assisted photonic engineering. The project is available at https://pcfbench.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: PCFBench: How Far Can Large Vision-Language Models Go in Physics-aware Photonic Inverse Design?

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents combine models with execution harnesses, so agentic benchmark performance reflects their joint behavior. We argue that harnesses should therefore be evaluated through their interactions with underlying models. We develop a framework combining five complementary measures: (i) Valid Completion Rate (VCR), how reliably agents finish normally and deliver evaluable results, irrespective of task correctness; (ii) Model-Harness Fit, how well a harness supports task achievement through valid completion for a given model; (iii) Cross-Model Fit, a harness's overall suitability across evaluated models; (iv) Interaction Residuals, pairing-specific execution strengths and weaknesses hidden by component-level summaries; and (v) Token Load, the token demands of agent execution, including failed attempts. We evaluate four general-purpose harnesses (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Pi CLI, and DeepAgents) with four core models, plus two fixed native model-harness systems, on six benchmarks covering context management, tool use, long-context planning, multimodal interaction, and artifact handoff. Including native references and stress conditions, 111 evaluation settings yield 52,168 trajectories. Harness rankings vary across models and benchmarks; task performance and valid completion can favor different pairings, and similar task scores can accompany distinct execution profiles. OpenCode ranks first in cross-model performance, while DeepSeek V4 Flash Preview maintains consistently high Mean VCR across harnesses on the shared four-benchmark panel. These findings support evaluating model-harness interactions, training transferable harness-use capabilities in models, and harness designs adapted to the model and task.
evidence_items.title: When Agents Fail: Model or Harness--Who's to Blame?

evidence_items.summary: Image generation models have rapidly advanced, with many models now supporting generation conditioned on multiple reference images and textual instructions. Such models enable a wide range of applications, including entity fusion and attribute transfer across images. However, existing benchmarks for multi-reference image generation rely on limited evaluation dimensions and fail to capture the diverse challenges of the task. To address this limitation, we propose MDMR-Bench, a Multi-Dimensional benchmark for Multi-Reference image generation. MDMR-Bench is organized around representative capability settings and consists of multiple evaluation subsets spanning diverse dimensions of multi-reference image generation, including (1) common entity fusion and attribute transfer, (2) multi-element extraction from a single image, (3) infographic manipulation, and (4) visual reasoning-intensive generation. This design enables systematic analysis of model capabilities and failure modes across different challenge dimensions. Furthermore, to achieve more reliable and interpretable evaluation, we introduce a checklist-based evaluation protocol that decomposes generation quality into fine-grained evaluation aspects. Instead of relying solely on holistic scoring, our framework uses structured checklists composed of both global-level and atomic-level queries, enabling more diagnostic assessment of model performance. By benchmarking both open-source and proprietary models, we demonstrate that MDMR-Bench provides fine-grained insights into model performance across different dimensions. The dataset and code are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: MDMR-Bench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Multi-Reference Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute tasks asynchronously: a main agent continues working while its subagents run, and the task state may change before their results arrive. The main agent must decide which work to update or preserve and which checks to repeat, while avoiding prohibited changes. Final task success alone does not reveal whether these results were handled correctly, and natural asynchronous arrivals are hard to reproduce. We introduce Async-RBench, a benchmark for asynchronous task execution in LLM agents, with 200 executable tasks covering eight scenarios. A scenario controller regulates result delivery using predefined task-state conditions, while an Event Response Contract (ERC) specifies what each response must change, preserve, avoid, and re-verify. The Dynamic Replanning Score (DRS) weights the response process and outcome equally and is reported separately from task success. We evaluate nine agents and find DRS scores of 19.2 to 45.1, with the lowest scores on duplicate reports and subagent failures. Under our execution protocol, all nine agents obtain lower task success with asynchronous than with batched delivery (26.0% vs. 29.7% on average). For three agents, prompting the main agent to rebuild its plan after every result improves DRS by only 2.6 to 3.5 points. Together, these findings highlight the challenges of reliable asynchronous task execution and the need to evaluate how agents handle incoming results alongside end-to-end task success.
evidence_items.title: Async-RBench: Benchmarking Asynchronous Task Execution in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: In unsupervised multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD), local variation can inflate reconstruction and forecasting errors, making observation-space discrepancy an unreliable indicator of abnormal system behavior. Since latent-space scoring can mitigate this limitation, we reframe one-class MTSAD as current-point system-state compatibility estimation and propose TENET, the Time-point Encoding Network for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection. We define the current-point system state as a latent representation of the target time point, constructed from variable-level temporal context in the input window. TENET constructs this state through a temporal layer that retrieves window context relative to the current point, encodes time with current-point-centered embeddings, and adaptively mixes the retrieved context with the current representation. With this design, TENET treats the input window not as the object to reconstruct, forecast, summarize, or score, but as context for constructing a latent representation evaluated with a fixed standard-normal negative log-likelihood score. Across benchmark datasets, TENET achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional experiments further show that TENET remains effective under alternative one-class objectives and outperforms substitutions based on generic sequence encoders, suggesting that its advantage comes from decision-aligned representation construction rather than from a specialized scoring rule. These results indicate that one-class MTSAD can be strong when the latent representation is designed around the current time point.
evidence_items.title: TENET: Time-point Encoding Network for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

evidence_items.summary: Multi-stage analytical tasks require LLM agents to use intermediate evidence to decide whether to continue, redirect or stop. Self-reflection, in which an agent critiques its output, is widely studied, yet a critique does not show whether evidence changed the next action. We call that capability self-restraint. Existing agent benchmarks largely measure task completion or output quality and leave it untested. DMAIC-Bench evaluates it with 97 seeded tasks across 15 industrial cases in four sectors, built around Lean Six Sigma's explicit statistical prerequisites. Paired counterfactual variants require opposite actions at the same workflow position, distinguishing warranted restraint from indiscriminate stopping. We assess execution traces with a private scorer and final claims through independent expert review. Across 13 models from six providers, execution-level routing accuracy averages 92% on matched GO decisions and 19% on NO-GO decisions, counting any forbidden downstream computation as a route error. Execution traces show agents reporting correct diagnostics before performing analyses that those results disallow. Separately, blinded expert review of the 11 audited agents estimates that reports act on invalid evidence at 47% of reached NO-GO decisions, with an interval from 31% to 61%. Explicit stopping permission helps some models without consistently restoring correct decisions at both GO and NO-GO forks. Sixteen life-sciences tasks in bulk ribonucleic acid sequencing (RNA-seq) and case-control genome-wide association studies (GWAS) show that the same framework can evaluate evidence-dependent decisions beyond industrial workflows. Project code and data are available at: https://github.com/psptpx/DMAIC-Bench-public.
evidence_items.title: DMAIC-Bench: From Self-Reflection to Self-Restraint for Agents in Multi-Stage Analytical Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Existing temporal video grounding (TVG) benchmarks primarily focus on localizing target video segments according to descriptive text queries of the visual content. However, real-world queries are more diverse and often require the model to first understand the user's intent before localization, such as finding visual evidence, identifying the cause of an event, or recalling a remembered moment, yet such queries remain largely overlooked. To mitigate this gap, we introduce RVG-Bench, a benchmark for reasoning-driven audio-visual temporal grounding, where every query is constructed such that the target segment can only be identified through reasoning about the query's underlying intent. We carefully construct the benchmark and rigorously verify its data quality to ensure models truly comprehend the audio-visual content. RVG-Bench comprises 1,255 videos and 1,890 query-interval pairs across eight reasoning types. We evaluate 22 models and find that the strongest, Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash, achieves only 49.6 mIoU. Through a series of controlled analyses, including oracle-grounding probes and test-time scaling experiments, we systematically examine where and why current models struggle, providing insights for future model development.
evidence_items.title: RVG-Bench: A Benchmark for Reasoning-Driven Audio-Visual Temporal Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Screen Tables and Substrate Scopes are information-dense figures widely used in synthetic chemistry literature, yet automated extraction of structured reaction data from them remains challenging. We introduce RxnExBench, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained reaction-level evaluation. Built from high-impact chemistry journals, it contains 3,565 expert-annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures. The dataset adopts a unified schema with 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields, supporting downstream AI-for-Chemistry tasks such as retrosynthetic planning, yield prediction, and reaction condition recommendation. RxnExBench further provides a reasoning-driven difficulty taxonomy, a modular annotation pipeline, and the Oracle-MolRec protocol, which disentangles molecular recognition from higher-level reasoning. Evaluation of 9 state-of-the-art VLMs shows that performance degrades substantially as schema complexity and reasoning demands increase. Under the Oracle-MolRec setting, results further reveal that accurate molecular recognition alone is insufficient, with multimodal integration and chemistry-aware reasoning remaining the primary bottlenecks. We release all data and code to facilitate future research in chemistry-aware multimodal understanding and AI-for-Chemistry dataset construction. The dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/opendatalab/RxnExBench.
evidence_items.title: RxnExBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Structured Chemical Reaction Extraction from Scientific Literature

evidence_items.summary: Continual survival analysis on whole-slide images (WSIs) requires models to integrate knowledge from sequentially arriving cancer cohorts while preserving previously learned information. Model merging offers a data-free alternative by combining independently fine-tuned task experts without retaining previous training data. However, the relative behavior of different merging strategies for WSI-based survival prediction remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we establish an end-to-end benchmark for data-free continual model merging, covering task-specific fine-tuning, sequential merging, and inference under both TASK-IL and CLASS-IL settings. We systematically evaluate six representative merging strategies across four TCGA cancer cohorts and three task orders using C-index, IPCW C-index, Forgetting, and Backward Transfer under a controlled protocol. Results show that no merging strategy consistently dominates across all evaluation criteria, while censoring-aware evaluation can substantially alter the relative ranking of the compared methods. This benchmark provides a unified foundation for developing and evaluating more effective continual model merging methods for WSI-based survival analysis.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Data-Free Continual Model Merging for Whole-Slide Image Survival Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Repository-level coding benchmarks largely assume that tasks and environments remain unchanged throughout execution. In software development, code, dependencies, runtime state, and requirements can change while an agent is still working. We introduce SWE-Shift, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under such mid-execution changes. From the same saved history and workspace, a Clean continuation proceeds without intervention, while a matched Shifted continuation receives a task-relevant update. Success requires completing the current task, preserving still-valid work, and satisfying the applicable state and evidence checks. The benchmark contains 120 scenarios across 12 change families, each evaluated at nine scheduled intervention positions. We evaluate 17 coding-agent systems, all of which have lower Shifted than Clean success. GPT-6 Astra drops from 67.35% to 24.79%, with 20.34% paired success. Tool/session changes and stale evidence yield zero paired success across all systems. Late-position paired success is lower for some systems and higher for others. These results show that success on the unchanged task can coexist with failures to preserve work, recover state, or refresh evidence after an update.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Shift: Evaluating Coding Agents in Evolving Workspaces

evidence_items.summary: This paper studies the problem of test-time robustness scaling for large vision-language models (LVLMs), which aims to mitigate language bias during inference. Existing approaches typically adopt test-time scaling techniques such as contrastive decoding to improve inference performance. Despite the progress, the performance of these approaches is far from satisfactory due to intentional evidence removal during perturbations and redundant inference cost. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Margin-gated Contrastive Debiasing with Evidence Restoration (MAGIC). The core of our MAGIC is to evaluate the decision margins of LVLMs to selectively activate textual and visual perturbation branches for efficient debiased inference. In particular, our MAGIC first measures the prediction margins of crucial tokens, and applies a gating function to identify low-confidence responses that are susceptible to language biases. For selected samples, we integrate the token logits from multiple textual and image perturbation branches with the original ones for debiased decision. More importantly, we selectively restore the most informative corrupted views with sharp prediction distributions for ambiguous samples after debiasing, enabling evidence recovery for discriminative decision-making. We further utilize a calibration dataset to actively identify and prune ineffective branches during contrastive debiasing for cost reduction. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed MAGIC in comparison with extensive baselines.
evidence_items.title: MAGIC: Margin-gated Contrastive Debiasing with Evidence Restoration for VLM Test-time Robustness Scaling

evidence_items.summary: Deploying language agents in real applications demands more than the right answer: an agent must execute a multi-step business process correctly, follow domain-specific rules, and interact with a user across a dialogue, where the gap between saying and doing is the gap between a satisfied customer and a real loss. We argue that a deployable-agent benchmark should jointly assess four facets: the outcome an agent reaches, the trajectory it takes, its operational viability, and its policy compliance. Customer relationship management (CRM), where mutable records meet operational rules and consequential effects, exercises all four. We introduce CRM-Agent-Bench, an execution-grounded benchmark of 555 stateful, multi-turn tasks across nine business domains and 36 capability tags. Each task supplies a task-specific executable contract drawn from checks over actions, arguments, order, response, target state, and protected state; success is the strict conjunction of the checks declared for that task. We evaluate the complete agent system through these contracts and report scored coverage, latency, and cost. Across sixteen systems evaluated on the audited final release, strict success spans 64.32% to 83.60%; the closely grouped leading systems nonetheless diverge sharply in cost and per-domain reliability. CRM-Agent-Bench offers an auditable framework for measuring contract-grounded business-transaction integrity and adherence to task-declared benchmark policies, with a portable structure designed for extension as models improve. Github repository: https://github.com/salesforce-misc/crm-agent-bench
evidence_items.title: CRM-Agent-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents in Stateful Enterprise Environments

evidence_items.summary: Vision language models (VLMs) have been increasingly adopted in consumer smart-home camera systems to interpret recorded videos and provide insights. However, video clips captured from smart-home cameras are different from curated web videos dominating existing VLM benchmarks. Smart-home video clips often do not contain subtitles or narration and are captured from different viewing angles, under various lighting conditions, and in diverse scenarios. However, the capabilities of the model in this domain, under sparse visual signals and limited context, are not fully assessed by existing VLM benchmarks. To close this gap, we introduce OpenHome, a visual-only, four-option multiple-choice benchmark for evaluating smart-home video understanding. It contains 2,254 questions on 1,118 real-world video clips and organizes 10 tasks into three capability levels. Perception evaluates visible content, Reasoning evaluates causal, spatial, and temporal relationships, and Insight evaluates subject intent, supporting evidence and appropriate homeowner responses. Based on the dataset, we describe the task design, data pipeline and evaluation protocol, and report results for 32 closed-source and open-weight VLMs. The best model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 81.2% overall accuracy. Frontier closed-source models outperform open-weight models on every level. The best closed-source model leads the best open-weight model by 16.3% on Perception, 22.4% on Reasoning and 37.4% on Insight.
evidence_items.title: OpenHome: From Perception to Insight in Smart-Home Camera Videos

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous tool-using agents (such as OpenClaw and Claude Code ) suffer from threefundamental systems bottlenecks during extended operation: (1) Context Rot, the progressive degradation of factual recall,temporal rule tracking, and safety policy compliance as historical scrollback and noisy tool logs accumulate in the prompt; (2)Linear-to-Quadratic Token Inflation, where standard chat APIs re-transmit the entire conversation history on every turn (O(n)prompt token accumulation and O(n²) attention compute) while frontier reasoning models consume hundreds of output tokens perturn; and (3) Open-Loop Unverified Execution, where conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) acts solely as apassive pre-generation filter with no post-generation causal verification or destructive tool-call veto. This paper presents the blackbox systems architecture, mathematical formulation, live Teacher–Student gateway telemetry, N = 10,000-document ablationbenchmarks, and independent multi-model peer assessments of QDAS Brain™ (Quantum-Dynamic Associative SynapticEngine).
evidence_items.title: QDAS Brain™: A Closed-Loop Sparse Associative Memory, Token Compression, and Autonomous Agent Arbitration Gateway — Empirical Benchmark at N = 10,000 Memories and Independent Multi-Model Systems

evidence_items.summary: The rapid growth of microdramas has increased demand for high-quality script production. Long-form microdrama script generation with LLMs requires both diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence. Our observations reveal that candidate continuations increasingly concentrate on fewer narrative mechanisms as generation progresses, while conventional retrieval may reinforce trope reuse and overlook historical information essential to future plots. To address these challenges, we propose DraMaze, a multi-agent pipeline that explores diverse causal paths through trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation. It further constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize, retain, and retrieve historical memories based on future narrative goals. We also introduce MiDramaBench, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating script logic and creative quality across different script lengths, together with causal-pattern metrics for narrative repetition and diversity. Experiments show consistent improvements across three backbone LLMs. For 60-episode scripts of up to 60k words, DraMaze reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and achieves a Logic score of 82.5, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 8.5 points.
evidence_items.title: DraMaze: A Multi-Agent Pipeline with Future-Aware Memory for Diverse Microdrama Script Generation

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning research on water cyber-physical systems (CPS) is constrained by datasets that are either real but chemically poor, or simulated but free of sensing noise and attacks. We present AquaSense-ICS, an open dataset and benchmark that co-registers (i) a 25.4 h recording window (8.0 h of recorded data, 26% coverage) from a Raspberry Pi 5 edge node (TDS probe and BME680 ambient sensor, 1-2 s sampling, 23,688 records), with (ii) a looped network of 13 nodes (10 junctions, 2 reservoirs, 1 tank) simulated in EPANET-MSX for six water-quality species, (iii) a parameterised library of cyber-attacks (false data injection, replay, denial of service, drift) and unintentional sensor faults with sample-level ground truth, and (iv) augmented and TimeGAN-generated sequences, flagged by an origin column. The attack, fault and water-quality labels are traceable to a seeded generator, a documented rule or a simulation input. We show that the most common way of benchmarking such hybrid data, random row splits and labels computed from the input features, yields near-perfect but uninformative scores (macro-F1 = 0.9998 for Random Forest), and we replace it with a leakage-aware protocol using chronological splits and held-out attack types rather than label reconstruction. Under this protocol, no model exceeds the constant "normal" predictor for attack classification (macro-F1 = 0.465), and the best detectors reach a mean AUROC of 0.64 on attack types unseen during training (0.35-0.93 depending on the type), leaving substantial headroom. Data and simulation files are released under CC BY 4.0 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23390541, and attack generators and benchmark code under MIT.
evidence_items.title: AquaSense-ICS: A Hybrid Real-Simulated Cyber-Physical Dataset and Leakage-Aware Benchmark for Smart Water Quality Monitoring and Attack Detection

evidence_items.summary: PGA-G: Selective Adaptation and Conformal Calibration for Speech Deepfake Detection This research software and experimental evidence archive accompanies a study on selective adaptation of speech deepfake detectors under changing deployment conditions. PGA-G introduces a framework combining prevalence-based adaptation gating, consistency screening to identify reference-dependent shortcuts, and conformal calibration of operating points. The approach determines when adaptation is appropriate and when a frozen detector should be retained. The study evaluates PGA-G using SSL-AASIST, XLSR-Mamba, and AASIST on the ASVspoof 2021 DF and ASVspoof 5 benchmarks. Release contents: The archive provides the original PGA-G research implementation, pre-registration and experimental protocol records, per-repetition evaluation results, machine-readable summaries, automated verification scripts, and reproducibility documentation. Verification: The package supports 160 confirmatory numerical comparisons, 20 additional numerical consistency checks, SHA-256 integrity verification, deterministic condition-level evidence exports, and byte-identical regeneration of the source-grouped summary. The archived numerical evidence can be verified without GPU access or speech-data downloads. Repeating full detector inference requires separately obtained benchmark datasets, third-party pretrained checkpoints, and compatible detector-specific software dependencies, as documented in the repository. Source repository: https://github.com/saed-alqaraleh/when-to-adapt-speech-deepfake-detector Version: 1.0.0 Licensing: Original PGA-G software is licensed under MIT. Original research records and statistical summaries are licensed under CC BY 4.0, subject to the rights described in the repository. Third-party datasets and model weights are not redistributed.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Rewilding is a landscape recovery approach that seeks to enhance the functioning of degraded ecosystems by reinstating natural processes, and it is increasingly being adopted by organizations and landowners. Despite its popularity, there is no accepted way to assess rewilding's impacts, which is due in part to inconsistent monitoring and evaluation. To address this gap, we developed a systematic map of a unique dataset combining academic and gray literature on monitoring and evaluation in rewilding case studies. We mapped definitions of success, study systems, methods of monitoring, and evaluation metrics for rewilding case studies to compare where the different strands of literature overlap and contrast in focus. We found that researchers and practitioners have been focused on different aspects of rewilding and that the limited recording of case study details and lack of robust experimental design make it difficult to pool and compare data. Researchers and rewilding practitioners face challenges in building a robust evidence base from which to evaluate rewilding outcomes. These challenges include resources as well as spatial and time constraints, which all limit the consistency of data gathering among projects. More comparisons across rewilding projects, better standardization of data collection and data recording methods, and increased collaboration between researchers and practitioners could help remedy these limitations. We developed recommendations for how to monitor and evaluate rewilded landscapes to improve data quality and availability. These include the broad adoption of low‐cost and scalable survey designs with greater focus on comparisons across sites and continued effort toward open‐source data storage.
evidence_items.title: Systematic mapping of monitoring and evaluation in rewilding

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: To assess the accuracy of OpenEvidence relative to six leading large language models (LLMs) in answering refractive surgery multiple-choice questions, and to compare their performance with users of the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) Basic and Clinical Science Course (BCSC) Self-Assessment Program . Setting: Not applicable. Design: Randomized questionnaire-based study using 225 questions from the refractive surgery section of the AAO BCSC Program . Methods: OpenEvidence and 6 LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-5, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, and Grok) answered the same set of multiple-choice questions. Their accuracy was defined as the proportion of correct responses. Performance from 1,983 BCSC Self-Assessment Program users served as a benchmark. Results: OpenEvidence achieved the lowest accuracy (76%) and performed significantly worse (P<0.05) than all six general-purpose LLMs. Claude achieved the highest accuracy (92%), followed by Grok (89.8%). ChatGPT-5, Copilot, and Gemini each scored an accuracy of 88%, and ChatGPT-4o achieved 86.2%. All models’ lower 95% confidence interval bounds exceeded the 60% passing threshold. The average score of BCSC Self-Assessment Program users was 77%. All general-purpose LLMs scored significantly higher than BCSC Self-Assessment Program users ( P<0.05 ), whereas OpenEvidence did not. Conclusions: OpenEvidence demonstrated significantly lower accuracy than the six evaluated general-purpose LLMs and did not exceed the BCSC Self-Assessment program user benchmark on this standardized refractive surgery multiple-choice assessment. This task-specific difference was not fully explained by response-format noncompliance and should not be interpreted as direct evidence of globally inferior medical knowledge or performance in open-ended clinical applications.
evidence_items.title: OpenEvidence versus Six Leading Large Language Models in Refractive Surgery: Does Curated Medical Evidence Confer an Advantage?

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into medical education, research, and clinical decision‐support applications; however, their ability to apply anatomical knowledge in clinically relevant surgical scenarios remains insufficiently studied. This study evaluated and compared the performance of six contemporary LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, and Manus) using 25 expert‐derived applied surgical anatomy scenarios relevant to plastic surgery. Scenarios were developed by an expert panel consisting of one associate professor of anatomy and two plastic surgeons. Responses were generated using a standardized prompt and assessed with a structured scoring rubric evaluating anatomical accuracy, clinical reasoning, completeness, and safety, with a maximum score of 10 points per question. Critical errors were additionally assessed. Significant differences in overall performance were observed among models (Friedman χ 2 = 43.51, p < 0.001). ChatGPT achieved the maximum aggregate score (250/250), followed by Gemini (248/250), DeepSeek (241/250), Copilot (240/250), Claude (235/250), and Manus (219/250). Critical errors were infrequent and were confined to a reconstructive vascular physiology scenario: DeepSeek, Claude, and Manus each demonstrated one observed critical error, whereas ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot demonstrated none. Although all evaluated models demonstrated excellent performance, clinically significant anatomical misconceptions persisted despite high aggregate scores. These findings demonstrate strong performance by the tested LLMs on this specific scenario‐based benchmark, while also identifying clinically meaningful anatomical errors in a subset of responses. Future evaluations should focus not only on overall accuracy but also on clinically meaningful error patterns that may influence surgical decision‐making.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models and Applied Surgical Anatomy: Evaluation of Anatomical Reasoning in Expert‐Derived Plastic Surgery Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Automated history-taking in telemedicine has to collect a structured record of a patient’s complaint over many turns while adapting to what the patient answers. MedAgent-RAG is a multi-agent system, implemented as a LangGraph state graph, which keeps an explicit clinical state the slots gathered so far, a ranked differential diagnosis, the questions already asked, the red flags detected, and the current questioning phase, and selects every question as a function of that state, before grounding its final assessment in clinical guidelines retrieved by a parent–child retrieval-augmented pipeline. Evaluated on the MediTOD corpus with a language-model patient simulator, the system raises BERTScore F1 from 0.68 to 0.84 over a single-shot baseline. Beyond that system description, we study history-taking itself as a network problem. From 231 annotated interviews, we build a bipartite network of symptoms and differential diagnoses whose links are statistically validated against a hypergeometric null model, its one-mode projections, and questioning-flow networks over the topics physicians ask about. The knowledge network separates into 8 syndromic modules (bipartite modularity 0.70, z = 5.4) and is less nested than a degree-preserving null model (z = −6.4): the knowledge an interview must cover is compartmentalised rather than hierarchical. Frequent symptoms such as cough and dyspnoea bridge those modules and carry little information about the differential, whereas rarer findings such as haemoptysis, dysphagia and weight loss carry most of it. Physician questioning separates into two phases: a clinical history followed by a social, family, and exposure history, and a first-order Markov model over topics is the most parsimonious description of how physicians move between them. We discuss what these results imply for the design of language-model interviewers.
evidence_items.title: MedAgent-RAG: an agentic retrieval-augmented system for adaptive clinical history-taking, with a network analysis of medical interviews

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Australian wheatbelt is divided into three main growing regions: the North (New South Wales and Queensland), the South (Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania), and the West (Western Australia). Using wheat yield data from the 2015–2022 multi-environmental trials (METs) conducted by the National Variety Trials (NVT), this study examines genotype-by-environment interactions (G×E) and trialling efficiencies, within and across regions. The North had the highest mean yield (390 gm-2) and the largest proportion of phenotypic variance explained by G×E (64%), while the West had the lowest yield (355 gm-2) and the lowest G×E contribution (44%). Despite regional differences, yield gains were approximately 1.4 gm-2 per year (or ∼ 0.5% annually) across all regions. The West also showed the highest repeatability (0.85 ± 0.02) and the lowest least significance difference (5% LSD, 22 gm-2 ± 1 gm-2) for a benchmark five-year MET, compared to the South (0.70 ± 0.04, 35 ± 1.4 gm-2) and the North (0.59 ± 0.05, 35 ± 1.4 gm-2). Modelling results were consistent across regions and indicated that 2 years of testing at 20 sites per year delivered efficiencies that could not be improved very much further.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Trialling Efficiency of the Australian Wheatbelt

evidence_items.summary: As LLM-based agents are deployed with increasing autonomy in real-world environments, a critical failure mode emerges: agentic misalignment, where agents choose harmful actions over failure. However, existing safety benchmarks primarily evaluate whether agents comply with explicitly harmful instructions, leaving the conditions that cause agents to choose harmful actions poorly understood. To address this limitation, we propose AM-Bench, a unified taxonomy and 35 scenario evaluation benchmark spanning seven industries for agentic misalignment grounded in the fraud triangle, a well-established criminological framework explaining goal-directed misconduct. We adapt this framework to agentic environments and construct our evaluation suite and detection systems along three dimensions: perceived threat, perceived opportunity, and reasoning. We operationalize each dimension into structured subcategories rooted in prior theory: five threat categories derived from the instrumental convergence thesis, seven opportunity categories drawn from the Emergent Strategic Reasoning Risks (ESRR) taxonomy, and a novel four-question binary reasoning framework synthesized from prior literature. Our evaluation of 10 frontier models reveals a 62-percentage-point gap in misalignment across scenarios, with Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro exhibiting the highest levels of agentic misalignment while Claude Sonnet 4.6 displays near-zero rates across all conditions. Our reasoning framework further reveals that models may exhibit harmful behaviours without explicit situational awareness or explanation, complicating both mitigation and detection. AM-Bench scenarios and code are available at https://github.com/AI4Collaboration/Agentic-Misalignment-Bench
evidence_items.title: AM-Bench: A Unified Taxonomy and Evaluation Suite for Agentic Misalignment

evidence_items.summary: Preprint with the routed circuits, verifier and search code. We revisit the qubit-routing benchmark of Li, Ding and Xie (SABRE, ASPLOS 2019): 26 circuits routed onto the 43-edge IBM Q20 Tokyo coupling graph, scored by the number of added gates (three per inserted SWAP). With the same circuits, graph and metric and an exact replay verifier, our routings need 12,087 added gates in total against SABRE's published 68,559 (82% fewer). On identical inputs, Qiskit 2.4.1 SABRE gives 64,137 (default) and 53,418 (heavy trials), and pytket 2.18.5 gives 35,685. On the 15 circuits reported in common by later routing papers on this device, the best published counts (HAIL, 2025) total 13,044 against our 9,312. Our count is lower on every circuit than every method we found (SAHS, MCTS, FiDLS, ILS, TWP, HAIL), with one tie. The routings come from a level-synchronous beam search over SWAP sequences, combined with SABRE-style forward-reverse passes to refine the initial mapping. The search code was written by a language-model agent inside an autonomous discovery loop (about three hours, about 21 USD of model usage). Beam search for routing is not new. The contribution is the measured gap on this widely cited suite, the exactly verifiable routed circuits, and an account of the discovery process. Caveats: far more compute per circuit than the baselines, a metric that ignores depth and fidelity, two regenerated QFT circuits, and the design graph rather than the physical device. Files: the preprint (PDF + LaTeX source, figures, bibliography); the 26 OpenQASM benchmark circuits with the QFT generator; qmap.py (QASM parser, coupling graph, exact replay verifier, SABRE reimplementation); routings/best combined.json (initial mapping and full operation sequence per circuit) with a per-circuit source map; the baseline script and its output; every proposer run's router code, drivers and notes; SHA-256 sums. Reproduce: python qmap.py verify routings/best combined.json (prints total g add 12087).
evidence_items.title: Beam search over SWAP sequences on the SABRE benchmark: 82% fewer added gates than SABRE and 29% fewer than the best published routings for IBM Q20 Tokyo, found by an autonomous agent

evidence_items.summary: The application of predictive artificial intelligence (AI) within Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) systems represents one of the most consequential and underexplored frontiers in contemporary educational data mining. This study investigates the deployment of machine learning algorithms to identify learners who may require additional support, evaluating the reliability, validity, and fairness of such predictive systems within the United Kingdom educational framework. Drawing on a structured literature synthesis spanning 2015–2025, a comparative analysis of seven machine learning algorithms including Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, and Neural Networks was conducted using datasets simulated from real-world SEND contexts. Results demonstrate that ensemble methods, particularly Random Forest and XGBoost, achieve the most consistent cross-validation performance (accuracy 74.3–77.5%), while simpler models offer greater interpretability. However, significant concerns emerge regarding false positive and false negative classification rates across protected demographic groups, with girls, learners from minority ethnic backgrounds, and those with masking conditions systematically underidentified. Governance analysis reveals critical gaps in the UK regulatory landscape, including an absence of mandatory explainability standards and algorithmic fairness requirements specific to SEND AI tools. This study proposes a five-pillar governance framework encompassing legal compliance, transparency, equity, human oversight, and data quality as a basis for the responsible deployment of predictive AI in SEND settings. Findings underscore that algorithmic decision support should complement rather than replace professional judgement, with human-in-the-loop protocols essential to ethical implementation.
evidence_items.title: Predictive Artificial Intelligence in SEND Systems: Evaluating Early Identification, Risk, and Governance Implications
