evidence_items.summary: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.
evidence_items.title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development

evidence_items.summary: Human preference is now central to the evaluation, guidance, finetuning, and ranking of text-to-image models. However, the susceptibility of human preferences to bias in image generation remains underexplored. We identify a key observation: for human faces, perceived attractiveness overrides image quality in preference judgments, even when comparing real photographs of comparable fidelity. In a controlled user study, annotators rank more attractive faces as higher quality, even when unattractive real faces are compared with attractive AI-generated ones. We examine the downstream consequences of this bias. Firstly, simulating Elo rankings from user study data shows attractiveness can distort a leaderboard's ranking, elevating synthetic attractive faces over real, unattractive ones. Secondly, the same bias reappears in the human preference models. Editing 40 annotated facial attributes in isolation, we find that attractiveness is the strongest correlate of score for four of five human preference models (PickScore, MPS, HPSv2.1, HPSv3), and the strongest predictor of score in regression analysis. We further show that preference aligned generation shifts faces toward younger, more feminine faces, and can override explicit prompts for unattractive faces, thereby limiting user control. Finally, we explore mitigation strategies, both for data collection and post training on human preference models. These findings highlight the need for preference models that disentangle image quality from human cognitive bias, enabling more reliable evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Attractive Faces Skew Text-to-Image Reward Models and Leaderboards

evidence_items.summary: Remote sensing agents rely on perception, measurement, and raster analysis tools to solve Earth observation tasks. We refer to their judgments and quantitative results about ground objects as tool observations. However, these observations are subject to uncertainty and may be incorrect even when tools execute successfully. When agents accept incorrect observations, the errors can propagate through subsequent reasoning and cause task failure. We analyze 1,229 execution trajectories across three remote sensing agent benchmarks. On each benchmark, at least 88.1 percent of tasks depend on tool observations. Among these tasks, at least 22.7 percent contain incorrect observations despite successful tool execution. These errors propagate to the final answer in at least 82.0 percent of affected tasks on each benchmark. To address this problem, we propose RSure-Agent, a framework for verifying tool observations and limiting error propagation. We introduce a verifiable observation protocol that requires tools to return process evidence for the agent to verify their observations. We construct a task-tool reliability prior from offline task feedback. The prior summarizes each tool configuration's past performance across task types and provides a task-specific reference for verification. Using process evidence and this prior, RSure-Agent decides whether to accept an observation, request additional evidence, or reject it. We evaluate RSure-Agent on EarthBench, ThinkGeo, TerraLogic, and CHOICE-420. Across three agent benchmarks, RSure-Agent reduces the error propagation rate by 21.3 to 25.9 percentage points relative to the base configuration with verification and the prior disabled. On CHOICE-420, it improves overall accuracy over direct answering by 5.71 percentage points on average across 11 backbone models. On EarthBench, it reduces the tool-call ratio by 25.9 percent relative to Earth-Agent.
evidence_items.title: RSure-Agent: Reliable Use of Tool Observations for Remote Sensing Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute multi-step workflows through tool use and interaction with users and environments. However, current agent evaluations are largely English-centric, limiting our understanding of agent capabilities in multilingual settings. We introduce BabelFlow, a benchmark-general agentic workflow that adapts existing agent benchmarks to new languages by analyzing runtime dependencies, coordinating structure-preserving translation, and combining multi-layer verification with human review to preserve task and evaluation semantics. Using BabelFlow, we construct BabelArena, a task-aligned benchmark comprising 16,146 instances derived from 702 canonical tasks across four benchmark families, 13 domains, and 23 languages. Experiments with five frontier models show that no single model dominates across benchmark families and that cross-language disparities extend well beyond task success. Lower-resource languages exhibit distinct failure patterns, with larger shares of tool-use and control-flow errors rather than answer-quality errors alone, pointing to gaps in reliable task execution across the resource levels of these languages. On the same tasks, agents in low-resource languages also consume substantially more tokens than in English (up to roughly twice the input) without proportional increases in interaction length, and language consistency degrades further on tasks requiring structured output, where switches are directed overwhelmingly toward English. We believe BabelArena provides a foundation for advancing research on reliable and efficient multilingual agents.
evidence_items.title: BabelArena: A Large-Scale Multilingual Benchmark for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs), an interesting question has emerged: how do LLM-based agents perform in Minecraft? To date, most Minecraft benchmarks evaluate them under fixed game mechanics, which are extensively documented online. High performance in these settings does not show whether an agent can continue making progress when familiar recipes, drops, and other rules change. In this paper, we introduce MirrorCraft, a paired benchmark for evaluating agents under hidden rule changes in Minecraft. Each Mirror world is a copy of its paired Vanilla world, with selected server-side rules silently modified by the datapack of one rule suite. Terrain, spawn, resource placement, task, interface, and action budget remain matched within every Vanilla-Mirror pair. MirrorCraft includes 10 Vanilla worlds in five controlled biomes, six rule suites, and three progression tasks, and we evaluate two LLMs and six agent configurations under a shared Mineflayer interface. We measure progress with server-verified advancement milestones and completion with success rate, and define the Rule Intervention Effect (RIE) as the performance change between paired Vanilla and Mirror worlds. Experiments with 8,640 episodes show that hidden rule changes have sharply different effects across suites. Among the configurations evaluated without rule descriptions, ReAct, Reflexion, and Voyager achieve the highest pooled Mirror Scores, but ReAct loses the most under compressed resource drops. Providing ReAct with the exact rules yields modest gains in average progress and completion across all three tasks, yet most of the difference between suites remains once the rules are known. MirrorCraft extends Minecraft evaluation beyond fixed mechanics and provides a controlled setting for studying how agents use gameplay outcomes when the rules of the current world differ from familiar ones.
evidence_items.title: MirrorCraft: Paired Evaluation under Hidden Rule Changes in Minecraft

evidence_items.summary: Explainability is an important requirement for machine learning models in high-risk domains such as medicine. We introduce HierViT, a hierarchical Vision Transformer that combines competitive predictive performance with multiple mechanisms to support the interpretation of its predictions. The model first predicts clinically relevant visual appearance attributes, which are then used to infer the final target prediction through a hierarchical reasoning process. To facilitate understanding of the intermediate representations, attribute-specific prototypes are visualized as representative image examples, while attribute-specific attention maps highlight image regions associated with each visual feature. Together, these attribute-level components provide complementary views of the model's reasoning by linking representative image examples and spatial attention to semantically defined visual features. We evaluate HierViT on two medical benchmark datasets: LIDC-IDRI for lung nodule assessment and derm7pt for skin lesion classification. Across both datasets, HierViT achieves competitive predictive performance while providing attribute-level prototypes and attention visualizations that support the interpretation of its predictions.
evidence_items.title: Hierarchical Vision Transformer with Prototypes for Interpretable Medical Image Classification

evidence_items.summary: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms.
evidence_items.title: RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

evidence_items.summary: Hyperspectral target detection (HTD) aims to locate and recognize objects at a fine-grained scale, playing a pivotal role in remote sensing. Despite significant progress, current HTD methods primarily focus on feature comparison while neglecting distribution learning for background-target separation, which can limit detection robustness in practical applications. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a spectral-wise conditional diffusion model that reformulates HTD as a task of generating a detection map. Specifically, we treat background and target confidence scores as training samples and use the corresponding pixel spectra as guiding conditions to capture the distributional discrepancy between background and target through diffusion and denoising. To enhance practical applicability, we propose a lightweight conditional denoising network based on multilayer perceptron to map noisy confidence scores to their ideal counterparts and adopt a deterministic reverse non-Markov chain to skip sampling steps, thereby accelerating the generation process. Furthermore, we introduce a composite loss to improve background-target separation. This loss integrates constrained energy minimization loss to enhance target saliency and suppress the background by maximizing the target response while minimizing average output energy, alongside binary cross-entropy loss to classify background and target using pixel-wise labels. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, with improvements in both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual effects.
evidence_items.title: SCDM-HTD: Spectral-Wise Conditional Diffusion Model for Hyperspectral Target Detection

evidence_items.summary: Hand landmarks serve as input for gesture recognition, sign language understanding, and touchless human-computer interaction. Yet hand pose estimators are typically evaluated with frame-wise localization metrics such as PCK or MPJPE, which are computed over matched predictions and overlook missed or spurious hands, handedness errors, and temporal instability. To address these limitations, we present VERA-Hand, a benchmark that evaluates estimators using manually verified, frame-level 2D annotations for 10,690 hands across four complementary dimensions (detection, localization, identification, and temporal stability), as well as a joint Pose-F1 metric that requires both correct detection and accurate localization. Evaluating six estimators spanning hand-specific, whole-body, reconstruction-based, and foundation-model paradigms, we find that no estimator dominates: rankings reorder sharply across dimensions. VERA-Hand also exposes failures that localization-only and downstream evaluations may not reveal, including cross-hand overlap in over 85% of frames for a recent foundation model. A post-hoc cleanup case study demonstrates how the benchmark can validate corrective interventions, while stratified analyses show that robustness varies across motion-blur classes and hand regions. We release the verified annotations, protocol, and code at https://gibranbenitez.github.io/VERA_Hand/
evidence_items.title: VERA-Hand: A Verified Multidimensional Benchmark for 2D Hand Pose Estimation in Third-Person Dynamic Gesture Videos

evidence_items.summary: While wide-angle lenses provide an expanded field of view (FoV), they exhibit severe nonlinear distortion near image boundaries, unnaturally stretching people in these regions. Existing methods mostly focus on facial regions, require high computational costs, and lack temporal modeling, resulting in incomplete full-body rectification, impractical real-time deployment, and noticeable inter-frame shakes. To tackle these issues, we propose \textbf{FastVC}, an efficient full-body video rectification framework driven by distortion-aware spatiotemporal learning. Grounded in lens physics, FastVC introduces a distortion-aware thin-plate spline (DA-TPS) module that nonlinearly remaps control points into a peripheral-dense layout, enabling more accurate geometric fitting without additional computational cost. We further develop a dual-level spatiotemporal learning scheme for causal and stable video rectification. At the model level, neighborhood spatiotemporal attention (NST) aggregates local context and selectively fuses historical features with low overhead. At the optimization level, sparse spatiotemporal supervision applies spatial alignment only to anchor frames, decoupling frame-wise accuracy from temporal stability. Besides, we contribute the first benchmark dataset for wide-angle full-body video correction. Extensive experiments show that FastVC achieves state-of-the-art rectification fidelity and visual stability at 57.0 FPS.
evidence_items.title: Distortion-Aware Spatiotemporal Learning for Real-Time Wide-Angle Video Rectification

evidence_items.summary: Training environments remain a major bottleneck for agents in data-driven scientific discovery. Existing collections of executable and verifiable training environments are small, and their construction remains difficult to scale. To address this limitation, we introduce Poseidon, an automated pipeline for generating diverse, verifiable training environments from scientific code repositories at scale. From the same repository budget, Poseidon extracts nearly 10 times as many training environments as a prior approach by decomposing scientific workflows into four complementary task types: Reproduction, Subflow, Completion, and Correction, where each type targets a distinct capability for scientific research. A recursive improvement loop further refines failed candidates and recovers otherwise discarded environments. Using Poseidon, we construct Pearl, a collection of 97,659 executable and verifiable environments from 7,110 public repositories spanning 10 scientific disciplines. To the best of our knowledge, Pearl is the largest and most broadly multidisciplinary collection of scientific-agent training environments to date. Qwen3.5 models (9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B) trained on Pearl achieve consistent gains across six challenging scientific-agent benchmarks. Overall, the scale and diversity of Pearl offer opportunities for training scientific discovery agents.
evidence_items.title: POSEIDON: Scaling Training Environments for Scientific Agents from Code Repositories

evidence_items.summary: Building Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) systems for high-value scenarios such as financial marketing requires large volumes of domain-specific dialogue data, which privacy regulations, annotation costs, and the need for expert labor make hard to obtain. User simulation offers a remedy, but existing methods target general-domain dialogue and exhibit two key limitations: insufficient modeling of domain-specific business processes and compliance constraints, and inadequate capture of the colloquial, spoken-language character of voice interactions. We propose ProfileSim, a profile-driven user simulation framework for financial marketing outbound calls. It jointly models user profiles---demographics and Big Five personality traits---and business profiles---intents reverse-engineered from real call logs---enabling fine-grained control over simulated behavior. The base model is fine-tuned on real voice dialogue data and refined by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with hierarchical rewards at the dialogue and utterance levels. Paired with a customer service agent integrating Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) constraints and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), ProfileSim achieves the highest colloquial naturalness, the strongest user profile adherence and the lowest agent score on long-tail intents among all evaluated user generators, while producing substantially shorter user utterances at comparable business compliance. The generated dialogue data is designed to support intent recognition training, agent evaluation, and rapid cold-start deployment.
evidence_items.title: Profile-Driven User Simulation via Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Rewards for Task-Oriented Dialogues

evidence_items.summary: The 3rd WEAR Dataset Challenge asks for an activity label for every one-second window of four unseen participants. Each window has 15 VideoMAEv2 frame embeddings, the accelerometer signal of one random limb, and the windows are shuffled. This report is an empirical analysis of one system built after the challenge deadline. Window classifiers are stacked with features averaged over per-participant graphs of video neighbours and scored successor candidates, and a mean-field style decoder with a soft count constraint per activity labels all windows of a participant together. The setting is offline and transductive, and the count constraint relies on each activity being performed once. In a participant-wise simulation with participant-level bootstrap intervals, stacking added 0.051 macro F1 over stage-1 fusion and the count constraint 0.011 (95% interval 0.006 to 0.017). A quadratic seam distance ranks the true same-limb successor first among about 720 candidates in 83.9% of cases, but adding it to the link model changed macro F1 by -0.0001 (-0.0006 to 0.0005). With the decoder settings and the mixing weight chosen inside the folds and the mislabelled spans left out of training, the system scores 0.936 in simulation (0.940 for participants who performed each activity once); the submitted configuration scores 0.938 (0.943). Per-participant scores range from 0.80 to 0.97. These results come from a non-nested stacking protocol that uses unlabelled features transductively, so they are not a fully inductive estimate. An oracle that averages the final unary scores over the true segments reaches 0.973, and 79% of the remaining errors involve the null class. On the private leaderboard, which no choice used, the selected Kaggle submission scored 0.9231 (public 0.9254, with bounds partly tuned there), and a later one with bounds chosen in simulation scored 0.9247 (public 0.9253).
evidence_items.title: An Error Budget for Shuffled Multimodal Windows in the 3rd WEAR Challenge: Stacking, Count Constraints and Seam Matching

evidence_items.summary: When LLM-powered agents interact, information is repeatedly shared, expanded, and forgotten, yet multi-agent evaluation typically focuses on final task outcomes. We study such interaction as claim-level information dynamics and propose RIVER, which decomposes agent outputs into atomic claims and evaluates three complementary dimensions: convergence, exploration, and retention. Convergence captures cross-agent claim correspondence and stance alignment; exploration captures semantic breadth and extension beyond the source; and retention tracks source preservation and the persistence of new claims across stages and lineages. We evaluate five interaction strategies on 40 controlled news-generation cases. Repeatedly pooled interaction promotes convergence but narrows the information space, whereas distributed relay yields broader, less shared information. Further comparisons show that method-specific constraints increase exploration while weakening convergence and retention. Our findings suggest that collective information dynamics are better explained by underlying information-flow mechanisms than by simple downstream performance.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Final Outcomes: Quantifying Claim-Level Information Dynamics in Multi-Agent LLM Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Advances in Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) have enabled increasingly seamless human-AI interaction, but their unified processing of heterogeneous modalities also expands the attack surface, allowing adversaries to exploit richer input compositions to circumvent safety alignment. To counter such risks, omni-modal guardrails have been proposed to detect and filter unsafe queries across arbitrary modalities. However, their capabilities and limitations remain insufficiently understood due to the absence of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. In this paper, we present Omni-UBench, the first comprehensive framework for omni-modal safety assessment, evaluating guardrail models along three critical dimensions, i.e., safety, utility, and reliability. Omni-UBench curates over 183k samples drawn from 35+ heterogeneous sources spanning text, image, audio, video, and their cross-modal combinations, annotated with safety labels under a unified risk taxonomy. Benchmarking under Omni-UBench on 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails yields several key findings, including: (1) modern OLLMs exhibit strong content moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; (2) existing guardrails still struggle to identify cross-modal queries that conceal harmful intent or involve sophisticated jailbreaks; (3) they further exhibit substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, revealing a deficient understanding of cross-modal safety semantics. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.
evidence_items.title: Omni-UBench: Benchmarking Omni-Modal LLM-based Guardrails Across Safety, Utility, and Reliability

evidence_items.summary: Contemporary large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems exhibit systematic advantages in deep research tasks, which emphasize iterative, vertically structured information seeking. However, when confronted with wide search tasks characterized by large-scale, breadth-oriented retrieval, existing agentic frameworks, primarily designed around sequential, vertically structured reasoning, remain stuck in expansive search objectives and inefficient long-horizon execution. To bridge this gap, we propose A-MapReduce, a MapReduce paradigm-inspired multi-agent execution framework that recasts wide search as a horizontally structured retrieval problem. Concretely, A-MapReduce implements parallel processing of massive retrieval targets through task-adaptive decomposition and structured result aggregation. Meanwhile, it leverages experiential memory to drive the continual evolution of query-conditioned task allocation and recomposition, enabling progressive improvement in large-scale wide-search regimes. Extensive experiments on five agentic benchmarks demonstrate that A-MapReduce is (i) high-performing, achieving state-of-the-art performance on WideSearch and DeepWideSearch, and delivering 5.11% - 17.50% average Item F1 improvements compared with strong baselines with OpenAI o3 or Gemini 2.5 Pro backbones; (ii) cost-effective and efficient, delivering superior cost-performance trade-offs and reducing running time by 45.8\% compared to representative multi-agent baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/mingju-c/AMapReduce.
evidence_items.title: A-MapReduce: Executing Wide Search via Agentic MapReduce

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents work in an environment that answers back: a compiler or test locates a faulty change, and version control keeps each change in a project that people can inspect, undo, and continue. Video editing agents, in contrast, act through interfaces designed for them rather than through the editor's own editing model: operation sets that cover only anticipated edits and are hard to compose, or scripts whose errors surface only in a rendered video that the user cannot keep editing. Neither the timeline nor the render cheaply tells them what each frame of the current edit shows. We present Cassette-Editor, which builds the agent's environment from the editor's own editing model, so that the agent edits the way the user does. Two domain tools make the timeline document the action language, in which edits are compositions of typed changes rather than separate tools. A rulebook shared with manual editing checks each patch like a compiler's semantic checker: the patch commits as one step of the shared history, or it is rejected without effect, with each problem located and repair options listed. Reads map source analysis, stored once in source time, to the frames of the current edit. A parity evaluation shows that every manual action the editor registers can be expressed as an agent patch that reaches the same independently specified document. In a whole-system case study of consecutive revisions to a long documentary rough cut, Cassette-Editor completed more of the judged requests than Codex CLI with the same model at similar cost; with a stronger model, under which both completed every request, it used fewer tokens and less agent time.
evidence_items.title: Cassette-Editor: A Video Editing Agent That Edits the Way You Do

evidence_items.summary: Background Image-based dietary assessment is useful for precision diabetes care. Multimodal Large Language Models (mLLMs) may greatly facilitate dietary self-monitoring. However, comprehensive evaluation of their real-world accuracy remains limited. Methods We developed SeeFood, an open-source benchmark, and evaluated eight commercial and open-source mLLMs on 80 real-world meal photographs from the SNAPMe dataset for nutrient and energy estimation (calories, carbohydrates, protein, fat, fiber), food-item identification, and day-level diet quality (Healthy Eating Index, HEI-2020). Three finalists were evaluated on the complete dataset (1680 photographs, 275 participant-days), and the best model was analyzed by meal type, portion size, sizing-marker use, ingredient visibility and meal complexity. Results GPT-4o mini achieved the lowest errors, with a significant advantage for carbohydrates; the three finalists performed similarly on other outcomes and on HEI-2020. Mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE) remained high (52%--90%), and the direction of bias was model-specific. The carbohydrate mean absolute error was 13.3 g (95% CI 12.4--14.3), and only 57% of meals were within +/- 10 g, a clinically relevant threshold for insulin dosing in type 1 diabetes. Calorie errors for lunch and dinner were in the range reported for human estimation on other images (~55% MAPE), whereas drink-only images had the highest relative errors (312% MAPE) because of dissolved sugars. Food items were reliably identified when fully visible (Dice = 0.74), and HEI-2020 estimates showed moderate agreement with reference values (RMSE = 12.5 points; r = 0.61). Larger portions were increasingly underestimated, and sizing references did not improve accuracy. Newer or larger models and chain-of-thought prompting did not consistently improve performance.
evidence_items.title: Image-Based Dietary Assessment Using Multimodal Large Language Models: Performance, Limitations, and Clinical Applicability in Diabetes

evidence_items.summary: High-resolution unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery is increasingly used for waterway inspection, but automated scene understanding remains constrained by the lack of pixel-level datasets that explicitly represent revetments and their complex interfaces with water, vegetation, roads, and riverside structures. We introduce the Riverway and Landscape Ground Dataset (RLGD), a dedicated UAV semantic segmentation dataset for waterway scenes. RLGD contains 100 images at 3000×4000 pixels, corresponding to 1.2 billion labeled pixels. Its public RLGD taxonomy explicitly includes revetment. Seven semantic segmentation models are evaluated under a unified protocol. Across five training runs with different random seeds, mean mIoU ranges from 69.27% to 77.02%, while Hierarchical Joint Network with Boundary Guidance (GHJNet) achieves 77.02 ± 0.41% mIoU and 83.51 ± 1.18% revetment IoU. Direct transfer from Varied Drone Dataset (VDD) to RLGD results in relative mIoU reductions of 11.29–49.81%, whereas adaptation using 20% of the RLGD training source images closes 65.5% of the measured domain gap. For the GHJNet run used in the downstream analysis, object-prior refinement using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) increases revetment IoU from 84.10% to 87.25%. A 42-image visual-completeness screening case study further achieves 83.93% macro-F1 and 81.25% balanced accuracy against image-level interpretations by three experts. Overall, RLGD provides a densely annotated, task-specific benchmark for dry-season waterway semantic segmentation, revetment extraction, and image-level inspection prioritization within the surveyed Yangtze River corridor.
evidence_items.title: RLGD: A High-Resolution UAV Dataset and Benchmark for Semantic Segmentation and Revetment Extraction in Waterway Scenes

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of Generative AI (GenAI) creates new opportunities for spatial planning. However, most existing applications focus on macro‐scale overhead perspectives, leaving street‐level visualization constrained by strict physical and spatial fidelity challenges. We introduce a controllable GenAI‐human interactive framework for producing spatially faithful and realistic street‐level imagery that reflects envisioned planning scenarios. Using Large‐scale solar photovoltaic (LSPV) site planning as a test case, it leverages vision‐language models to integrate human inputs (e.g., textual intent, scribbles) and existing status photos, synthesizing photorealistic outcomes. To support systematic evaluation, we constructed a large‐scale street‐view imagery dataset of before‐and‐after solar panel installation across the United States. We comprehensively evaluated 11 model settings covering five open‐sourced diffusion models and one commercial vision foundation model to test fidelity and realism. Our study illustrates how a GenAI‐human interactive pipeline can support visualizing proposed environmental interventions, and offers a benchmark for conditioned GenAI visualization applications.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Planning Scenario Visualization: A Framework and Benchmark for Controllable Street‐Level Image Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Hybrid quantum–classical neural networks are reported to classify brain tumors on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) accurately, but these reports rarely control for data leakage or test whether the quantum circuit contributes. We examined both issues. Methods: We audited version 2 of the Kaggle Brain Tumor MRI Dataset (7200 images) with mirror- and rotation-invariant duplicate detection and by matching every image to its source collections, which recovered patient identities for 4846 tumor images. A variational quantum circuit (VQC) was compared with size-matched, deeper and Fourier-surrogate classical controls using frozen features, end-to-end fine-tuning and training from scratch, all under patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation. Results: Of the 1600 test images, 1269 (79%) had a copy in the training partition, and 915 of the 917 figshare-derived test images shared a patient with it. On frozen features, a six-qubit VQC head was 6.0 percentage points (pp) less accurate than its classical control (95% confidence interval −6.8 to −5.2) and less accurate than a classical surrogate of its own function class. With fine-tuning, it stayed within about 1 pp of its control but was 0.7 pp less accurate (−1.2 to −0.1) after convergence-based training; a hybrid network trained from scratch was 8.3 pp less accurate than its control. Patient-grouped evaluation lowered accuracy by 3–8 pp relative to our earlier duplicate-grouped evaluation, and 76 glioma test images from another source remained poorly recognized. Conclusions: The quantum layer added cost but no accuracy, and leakage and provenance mattered more than the classifier head.
evidence_items.title: Does the Quantum Layer Help? A Leakage-Aware Benchmark of Hybrid Quantum–Classical Models for Brain Tumor MRI Classification

evidence_items.summary: Background/Aim: Deep learning models can achieve high accuracy in colorectal histopathology classification, but their performance may decrease under adversarial perturbations. This study aimed to evaluate the adversarial robustness of a 2D-CNN across two colorectal histopathology datasets under FGSM, PGD, and BIM attacks and to compare adversarial training with convolutional autoencoder (CAE)-based input purification as defense strategies.Methods: Experiments were conducted on the Kather Texture 2016 and CRC-VAL-HE-7K datasets, containing 5,000 and 7,180 image patches from eight and nine colorectal tissue classes, respectively. A 2D-CNN was trained using five-fold stratified cross-validation and evaluated on held-out test sets. White-box FGSM, PGD, and BIM attacks were applied across multiple perturbation levels. Adversarial training was examined using three clean-to-adversarial training compositions. For input purification, shallow, deep, and mixed-ε deep CAE models were evaluated. Performance was assessed using accuracy, macro precision, macro recall, and macro F1-score. Results: The 2D-CNN achieved 87.70% and 89.35% clean test accuracy on Kather Texture 2016 and CRC-VAL-HE-7K, respectively, but performance declined markedly under adversarial attacks, particularly on CRC-VAL-HE-7K. Adversarial training substantially improved robustness at ε = 0.01, although the best training composition varied across datasets and attacks. Mixed-ε deep CAE generally provided the strongest purification performance at higher perturbation levels. Conclusion: Despite its clean-image classification performance, the 2D-CNN remained vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Both defense strategies generally improved performance under the evaluated adversarial conditions: adversarial training substantially improved performance at ε = 0.01, whereas mixed-ε CAE purification generally showed stronger relative performance at higher perturbation levels.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Adversarial Robustness in Deep Learning-Based Colorectal Histopathology Classification

evidence_items.summary: TroPhish investigated how well freshwater fish feeding data could be integrated with Fish-base's species, ecology, diet, and nutrient component tables. It also explored how open datasets downloaded from Fish-base could be used to model fish feeding groups, feeding diversity, and trophic levels. For the analyses, 54,750 raw feeding records and 4,571 sample-level specified "fish ID" units were used as the basis. Fish-base matching was successfully completed for 88.6% of samples and 84.2% of species. This research led to the addition of "SpecCode" and "FamCode" to 4,051 samples, feeding-based trophic levels to 3,280 samples, and nutrient data to 3,440 samples for analysis. In the "Species Group K-Fold" validation, the Random Forest model was applied and enhanced with Fish-base datasets. In the feeding group classification, the trophic identification scenario achieved 0.515% accuracy, 0.397% balanced accuracy, and a 0.390% macro F1 score. In the training data, the model's generalizability to uncharacterized families was poor. The low performance in the "Family Code Group K-Fold" validation of the same scenario is evidenced by this. While the relational power of the feeding breadth regression was found to be limited (maximum R² = 0.092), the trophic level regression based on fish-based data yielded realistic findings in the taxon-trait scenario (R² = 0.403). The results suggest that the misleading signal related to fish feeding habitat is amplified by the inclusion of TroPhish and fish- based data. Model outputs are not an automated feeding classification system that produces definitive results. They should be considered as descriptive findings generated from research-driven modeling and publicly available data.
evidence_items.title: Estimation of fish feeding groups, dietary breadth and trophic levels based on open data through the integration of TroPhish and FishBase data

evidence_items.summary: Modern Security Operations Centers (SOCs) increasingly need autonomous response: not only detecting intrusions but deciding, in real time, how to react. Progress on learned response policies is held back by the absence of public datasets that pair a detection state with a defensive action and a measured outcome. We present SOC-RL, a reinforcement-learning dataset of State→Action→Reward→Next-State transitions collected on a live, containerised cyber range that extends the multi-layer detection SOC of the SOC-MLD dataset [1]. The environment exposes a 12-dimensional state built from live NIDS (Suricata) and web-server telemetry, a deployable action space (monitor, honeypot-redirect, hard-block) executed for real through the SOC's control API, and a multi-objective reward balancing attack containment, service availability and false-positive avoidance. We release 7,322 transitions over 1,800 episodes gathered under a multi-vector attack campaign with concurrent legitimate traffic, across three deployment conditions (distinct addressing, shared NAT addressing, and source-IP rotation), with the behaviour policy's action propensities logged for off-policy learning. Beyond an offline Fitted-Q baseline, our central result is a comparison of off-policy value estimates (FQE) against on-policy returns measured on the live range, and a demonstration that the “block the source” heuristic — trivially optimal in the usual single-address setting — becomes the worst active choice under shared NAT addressing, where it attains full containment but drives benign availability to zero. We further benchmark conservative offline-RL algorithms (CQL, BCQ) against an offline-DQN baseline on the same estimator. SOC-RL thus isolates the gap between what offline estimation promises and what a deployed policy delivers, and the sensing/action-space requirements a real autonomous responder must meet.
evidence_items.title: SOC-RL: A Live-Range Dataset of Measured Defensive Transitions for Autonomous SOC Response

evidence_items.summary: The transition to a green economy requires investment mechanisms that combine environmental objectives with commercially viable projects and credible institutions. This study examines how competitive procurement, payment guarantees, long-term contracts, and development finance can support international investment, using Uzbekistan’s solar energy sector as an empirical case. The research applies comparative project analysis to three solar projects, examines the disclosed financing structure of the Samarkand–Jizzakh investment package, and conducts an illustrative sensitivity analysis of financing costs. Calculations show that the average awarded electricity tariff for the two subsequent projects was 32.55% below the Navoi benchmark. The Samarkand–Jizzakh package combined USD 193 million in sponsor equity and USD 216 million in development-bank debt, alongside payment guarantees of up to USD 12 million. These findings document the coexistence of competitive tariffs, foreign participation, and coordinated risk mitigation; they do not establish a causal effect of guarantees or procurement reform. The article proposes an integrated investment mechanism linking project preparation, transparent procurement, targeted financial support, grid readiness, and environmental verification. Its principal contribution is a practical framework for evaluating investment attraction through financial closure, fiscal exposure, and verified environmental performance.
evidence_items.title: IMPROVING MECHANISMS FOR ATTRACTING INTERNATIONAL INVESTMENT DURING THE TRANSITION TO A GREEN ECONOMY

evidence_items.summary: Overview This dataset provides a frozen, SHA-256-verified collection of 224 historical James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) MIRI spectroscopic FITS products , assembled to support the reproducible execution of the Law et al. (2023) and Law et al. (2025) scientific benchmark workflows implemented in JWST-RCA V2 (Residual-Covariance Advisor). The dataset preserves the exact historical product bytes required by the benchmark manifests, addressing reproducibility problems that may arise when calibrated products in the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST) are subsequently reprocessed or replaced. Dataset Contents The archive contains 224 FITS files , organized into two benchmark collections: Law et al. (2023) — 24 products 12 MIRI/MRS S3D spectral cubes. 12 MIRI/MRS X1D extracted spectra. Law et al. (2025) — 200 products 200 MIRI/MRS X1D extracted spectra. All 224 files were recovered from preserved research archives and independently checked against the expected SHA-256 digests recorded in the frozen JWST-RCA benchmark manifest. The original FITS contents have not been modified, recalibrated, or scientifically transformed. Scientific Purpose The dataset is intended to support reproducible investigations of: Residual covariance and correlated spectral noise. Covariance and resampling behaviour in JWST/MIRI spectroscopic products. Spectroscopic repeatability and empirical uncertainty. Comparison between observed diagnostics and published external benchmark controls. Reproducibility of scientific analyses across software installations and historical calibration products. Preserving the original calibrated products is particularly important because JWST archive reprocessing may produce files with unchanged filenames but different contents, dimensions, calibration metadata, or SHA-256 values.
evidence_items.title: JWST/MIRI Historical Frozen Dataset for Reproducible Law et al. (2023, 2025) Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Mastering projection methods—specifically orthographic, axonometric, and perspective drawings—forms the fundamental cognitive baseline of architectural education. However, novice architecture students consistently struggle to translate 2D orthographic projections into 3D spatial reality, resulting in high cognitive load and visual misinterpretations. This study proposes and evaluates a novel Four-Stage Hybrid Pedagogical Framework that integrates traditional Monge orthographic projections with physical model-making, 3D Building Information Modeling (BIM), and 1:1 scale Virtual Reality (VR) spatial audits. Conducted over a 14-week academic semester with 120 first-year architecture students divided into three pedagogical cohorts (Control, Experimental A, Experimental B), performance was quantitatively assessed using the Revised Purdue Spatial Visualization Test (PSVT:R) and an orthographic error detection benchmark. Results indicate that Experimental Group B (2D + BIM + VR) achieved a 61.7% mean increase in spatial visualization scores (PSVT:R score increased from 14.1 to 22.8, p < 0.001) and attained an 89.6% accuracy rate in complex orthographic error detection while reducing drawing execution time by 47.5%. These empirical findings prove that immersive 3D/VR verification significantly reduces cognitive friction, establishing a more intuitive, scalable, and highly effective methodology for modern architectural graphics instruction.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing Projection Teaching Methods in Architectural Education: A Hybrid Pedagogical Framework

evidence_items.summary: This study proposes a methodological framework for analyzing public transit user satisfaction by processing unstructured, voice-derived trip chain data. Traditional survey methods often do not capture the contextual and real time aspects of user experience. To address this limitation, this study employs large language models and natural language processing techniques to analyze trip-related feedback collected from 5,000 public transit users. Sentiment scores were extracted from a station-labeled subset of the data set and applied to a broader corpus to assess satisfaction levels across subway stations in the Seoul Metropolitan Area. Using a combination of sentiment analysis and K-means clustering, this study categorized 102 subway stations into three groups: (1) High Satisfaction Station Group; (2) Low Satisfaction Station Group; and (3) Moderate Satisfaction Station Group. These clusters were the basis for grouping stations, and user feedback on transit experiences was summarized for each station within its respective cluster. This approach enables the identification of low-satisfaction transit stations requiring immediate attention, as well as moderate-satisfaction transit stations where service equity must be addressed. The proposed methodology offers a practical alternative to traditional survey-based assessments by leveraging unstructured public transit users’ data. With further refinement and institutional support, this approach can enhance data-driven, user-centered transit planning and contribute to broader improvements in urban mobility.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Based Sentiment Analysis for Public Transit Satisfaction Using Trip Chain Data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Patients increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for health information, yet the evaluation of the quality of fecal incontinence (FI) content from these models is limited. We aimed to evaluate the quality, understandability, and actionability of LLM responses to FI queries. We hypothesized that LLMs would provide variable quality responses with variable understandability and actionability. Methods Search data was extracted from Google Trends’ top five search queries related to FI to create identical prompts used to generate responses from four LLMs: ChatGPT version 4o mini (OpenAI), Perplexity version sonar (Perplexity AI), LLaMA version 3.2 (Meta AI), and Gemini version 2.0 flash (Google). Responses were assessed using DISCERN, Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT), and the Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Statistical analysis was performed using R version 4.4.2 (R Core Team, 2025). Results Response quality was moderate (median DISCERN 44 out of 80), nominal understandability was median 77% ([7/9] PEMAT) although inter-rater agreement was poor, and actionability was poor (median 40% [2/5] PEMAT). DISCERN scores varied significantly ( p = 0.033). The responses were at the high school to college level using the FKGL score. Readability differed significantly ( p = 0.022). Conclusions LLM responses demonstrated structural clarity using PEMAT criteria but lacked actionability and were above the recommended reading level for consumer health information. Continued evaluation of artificial intelligence is essential before LLMs can be recommended for patient education.
evidence_items.title: Quality, understandability, and actionability of large language model responses to fecal incontinence: a cross-sectional study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Mentalization - the ability to infer others’ beliefs and intentions to guide one’s own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.
evidence_items.title: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Simulating human mobility is crucial for urban planning, environmental exposure assessment, and social behavior studies. However, existing methods often rely on rules and assumptions, making it difficult to provide robust results and explicit decision‐making processes when generating plausible daily activity trajectories from sparse location records such as check‐ins. To bridge these gaps, we propose a large language model (LLM)‐based agent framework that innovatively incorporates the Chain‐of‐Thought (CoT) approach and Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) mechanisms, namely Daily mobility LLM (DaiLLM). This framework consists of three modules: the Profiler derives user characteristics from historical trajectory data; the Generator simulates movement through the CoT process, which integrates constraints from Profiler outputs; and the Discriminator employs RLAIF to evaluate the similarity between generated results and real data, providing feedback to optimize the results. Experiments demonstrate that: (1) our method improves accuracy by 34.2% compared to traditional approaches in daily activity trajectory generation; (2) the CoT approach enhances activity logic and results in a 26.1% increase through task decomposition and constraint integration; (3) the RLAIF mechanism explicitly provides an optimization process through Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) analysis; and (4) our method excels in transfer learning and long‐term generation across different city contexts. This study provides a robust, transparent, and cost‐effective solution for plausible daily activity trajectory generation from sparse check‐in data, which will establish a new paradigm for mobility behavior analysis in data‐scarce scenarios.
evidence_items.title: DaiLLM: An Agent Framework Based on a Large Language Model and Reinforced by AI to Generate Daily Activity Trajectories

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise in supporting drug recommendations both within and outside clinical settings, but they may also amplify systematic biases affecting equity and cost. We examined the commercial neutrality of LLM-generated product name recommendations among US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved products containing the same active ingredient. We evaluated product name recommendations from five LLMs using 177,120 synthetic clinical vignettes spanning 123 disease–drug pairs and 1,440 sociodemographic profiles. Each vignette specified a disease and an active ingredient and asked the model to recommend FDA-approved products. Across disease–drug pairs and models, the most frequently recommended product accounted for a mean of 97.5% of first-choice recommendations, and the models showed almost perfect agreement on which products to recommend. LLM-recommended product distributions differed from real-world prescribing patterns and often yielded higher projected acquisition costs. Recommendations inconsistent with regulatory information varied across LLMs and sociodemographic factors. Models more often recommended products with greater online visibility (Google search counts, odds ratio (OR) 1.70; a dedicated Wikipedia page, OR 3.00) and favoured originator products (OR 20.5), whereas products with later FDA approval and those more commonly prescribed in practice were recommended less often (ORs 0.76 and 0.87, respectively). Although modified prompts shifted recommendations in the intended direction, LLMs still favoured a narrow set of products, which could have potential implications for drug costs and pharmaceutical markets. Rigorous evaluation and targeted mitigation are needed before widespread use.
evidence_items.title: Large language models show product name convergence in drug recommendations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract In the legal domain, judgement prediction is an important and challenging problem. In real-life proceedings, judicial decisions depend on the precise presentation of complex case information and, above all, on the argumentative interplay among petitioners, respondents, and judges. However, most existing research work on this judgment prediction primarily focuses on case facts, rather than on argumentative legal reasoning. Furthermore, many such approaches rely on single-agent Large Language Models (LLMs), which are not analogous to the real-life courtroom. To address this limitation, simulating a courtroom conversation becomes essential. Some prior studies explored multiple LLMs (multi-agent) based courtroom simulations, with limited investigation on the quality of argumentation. Motivated by this crucial gap, in this work, we propose simulating courtroom arguments employing a multi-agent conversational system, termed as \naam, specifically tailored to crime-related cases. We consider solely legal cases from the U.S. Supreme Court, evaluating the ability of LLMs in generating courtroom arguments using different in-context learning approaches, including zero-shot, and the variant of few-shot techniques, within a multi-agent setup. Empirically, we find that the quality of arguments improves significantly when using local precedent retrieval based approach employing GPT-4o models. This strategy yields 12$%$ improvement over the zero-shot (baseline) setup. Subsequently, to measure the quality of LLM-based arguments, we propose a new algorithm -- coined as ArguEval. Eventually, to showcase the efficacy of generated arguments, we utilize them in a downstream \texttt{judgment prediction} task, which results in a 14$\%$ performance gain over the zero-shot baseline.
evidence_items.title: ArguGenCourt: Courtroom Argument Generation using Judicial Multi-agent Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present an automated framework employing large language models to categorize atomic spectroscopy literature for NIST bibliographic databases. The system processes native PDFs and supplementary materials via instruction-driven reasoning agents to assign structured search keywords encompassing target species, subject codes, and experimental methodologies. Validation against human-curated datasets demonstrates high precision in elemental species identification, while establishing that granular subject code assignment remains the primary source of categorization error.
evidence_items.title: Categorization of scientific publications using large language models as applied to atomic spectroscopy

evidence_items.summary: This study aims to evaluate the implementation of digital Arabic language learning among students enrolled in an Arabic Language Education Study Program at a state university in Makassar, Indonesia, using the Context, Input, Process, and Product (CIPP) evaluation model. This study employed a qualitative evaluative approach, with the head of the study program, lecturers, and students participating as research participants. Data were collected through observation, in-depth interviews, and document analysis. The data were analyzed using the interactive model developed by Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña, comprising data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that, in the context dimension, the implementation of digital Arabic language learning aligns with the needs of digital transformation and the demands of twenty-first-century education. In the input dimension, digital infrastructure, institutional support, and lecturers’ competencies were generally adequate, although variations in students’ digital literacy remained evident. In the process dimension, digital learning facilitated student interaction, participation, and flexibility in learning. In the product dimension, the implementation contributed to improvements in Arabic language proficiency, learner autonomy, and students’ digital literacy. Overall, the findings indicate that the implementation of digital Arabic language learning was generally effective and warrants further development. This study recommends strengthening technological infrastructure, providing continuous digital literacy training, and optimizing the integration of digital technologies and artificial intelligence into Arabic language learning.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming disaster risk reduction and management by enhancing prediction, preparedness, response, and recovery. Leveraging techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and foundation models, AI can analyse diverse datasets, including satellite imagery, sensor networks, social media, and historical disaster records, to improve early warning systems and risk assessments. AI applications range from predictive modelling of floods, earthquakes, landslides, and tropical cyclones to real-time damage assessment using computer vision and drones, and optimised emergency response planning. Additionally, AI supports post-disaster reconstruction and long-term recovery through economic modelling, infrastructure planning, and psychological support. Despite these benefits, challenges such as data scarcity, algorithmic bias, privacy concerns, and infrastructure requirements must be addressed to ensure equitable and effective deployment. Incorporating ethical frameworks, community engagement, and transparency is essential for maximising AI’s potential in building resilient communities and mitigating the social, economical, and environmental impacts of disasters.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Risk Management

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The environmental comparison of artificial intelligence (AI) systems is context-dependent regarding lifecycle boundaries, the sharing and allocation of infrastructure, the accounting of electricity use and the accounting of water use. A low operational carbon value can coexist with substantial upstream water consumption or a large unallocated hardware burden. This paper develops a lifecycle framework in which primitive resource events are assigned once to workload stages and translated into energy, greenhouse-gas, and water inventories through explicit, versioned factors. The framework separates physical water consumption from scarcity characterization, operational electricity from upstream energy carriers, and attributional reporting from consequential scheduling. We derive conservation under allocation, an exact temporal aggregation bias identity, an identifiability condition for incomplete inventories, a shared-infrastructure allocation model, and a service-volume break-even condition. A constrained minimax routing extension evaluates conflicting operational objectives without collapsing physical units into an unexplained score. A fully specified synthetic study covers three hypothetical regions, 168 hourly intervals, 24 demand profiles, four routing policies, and 10,000 uncertainty draws. For the base case of 3.36 million requests, carbon-only routing reduces serving carbon by approximately 50.5% relative to the reference, but increases serving water consumption by approximately 124.3%. Once fixed lifecycle burdens are included, the corresponding changes are approximately − 4.2% and + 9.6%. Through this specific situation, the minimax policy is redefined, so no enhancement over the minimax reference is claimed. This study does not exhibit accounting accuracy but rather accounting consistency and conditional decision behavior.
evidence_items.title: Lifecycle Intelligence for Carbon Energy Water Footprint Optimization in Artificial Intelligence Systems

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) offers significant potential to accelerate drug discovery, yet its adoption remains constrained by interdependent technical, organizational, and regulatory barriers. This study applies Fuzzy DEMATEL to analyze twelve challenges and uncover their causal structure using expert judgments expressed as triangular fuzzy numbers. Following normalization and CFCS defuzzification, Resistance to Change, Lack of Standardization, Limited Trust in AI Outputs, Talent Shortage, and Lack of Clinical Validation emerge as the primary causal drivers. These upstream barriers exert strong influence on downstream effects, including Regulatory Barriers, Biological Complexity, Integration with Legacy Systems, and Poor Data Quality. The findings indicate that several constraints commonly viewed as external are, in practice, manifestations of internal organizational and technical shortcomings. By providing a structured causal prioritization of barriers, this study offers actionable guidance for targeting high-leverage interventions in AI-enabled drug discovery. Findings reflect expert judgment within a North Cyprus context and should be interpreted as indicative organizational signals rather than universal prescriptions.
evidence_items.title: Mapping interdependencies among challenges to artificial intelligence adoption in drug discovery

evidence_items.summary: Scientific priors speed up Bayesian optimisation in materials discovery, but a prior that steers a small budget toward the materials it favours may miss those it disfavours. We measured this in a benchmark with a registered analysis plan: 7,020 searches (3,000 of them over 3,550 metallic multielement Materials Project structures), for the shear modulus and the specific Young’s modulus, with a historical prior and a composition-only elemental-modulus heuristic, each mixed into expected improvement search with a fixed weight β. Coverage was the recall of the half of the top-5% materials that the prior itself scores lowest. Coverage loss at moderate weight was detected in 4 of 6 prior–objective settings. The elemental heuristic reduced the restricted mean number of acquisitions to a top-1% shear-modulus material by 13.9 at β = 0.25 with no detected loss of coverage, but its shear-modulus form, applied to the specific modulus, lost 44.0% or more of the baseline coverage at every nonzero weight. A weight both beneficial and safe under the registered criterion existed in 3 of 6 settings (2 under a post hoc joint error control), never above β = 0.25, and depended on the safety margin and on curation. At β = 0.5, in 5 of 6 settings the weighted search found more top-5% materials in total but, by its estimates, fewer of those its prior disfavours (a loss detected in 3): the prior redirected the search rather than reducing its yield. Faster discovery alone therefore does not show that a search keeps what its prior disfavours.
evidence_items.title: The efficiency–coverage trade-off of scientific priors in Bayesian search: a registered benchmark on metallic multi-element elasticity data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present the data quality (DQ) report builder toolkit, DQRbuild , a suite of DQ tools that have been developed to vet gravitational-wave (GW) events in preparation for the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run. We explain the main functionality and the many scientific tests that we support. To validate the performance of the tools included in the toolkit, we run a series of tests on all significant candidates shared as public alerts in the third observing run to compare against what was manually reported using human intervention. We find that these automated tools can now identify 96% of the problems identified by humans during this previous observing run, with a 24% false alarm rate. We conclude with a commentary on the prospects and potential challenges for fully automating the process of vetting the DQ for GW events identified in future observing runs.

evidence_items.summary: Internal validation sub-studies compare an observed imperfect measurement of a variable with its gold standard measurement in a sample of participants. The gold standard is often expensive or difficult to collect, so the validation sample is usually small. We simulated a small cohort study with a nested, balanced validation sub-study and used the simulated cohorts to evaluate three analytic strategies with the objective of determining which of them, alone or in combination, improved the performance of quantitative bias adjustments informed by the validation sub-study. The strategies were: (1) incorporating a weak prior to the beta distributions assigned to the bias parameters, as opposed to no prior (2) restricting beta distribution assignment to the three predictive values informed by sampling, as opposed to all four predictive values, and (3) restricting imputation of gold-standard measurement to study cohort members who were not sampled for the validation sub-study, as opposed to imputing for all members of the study cohort. All twelve combinations of bias adjustment strategies returned bias-adjusted estimates with less bias and higher coverage than the simulated misclassified cohorts, although all had higher root mean squared errors and wider intervals because of the uncertainty added by incorporating the sparse validation data into the analysis. We found that assigning a prior may sometimes have utility, whereas restricting assignment of beta distributions for use only with sampling and restricting imputation to only cohort members not selected for the validation study adds computational complexity with little utility in return.
evidence_items.title: Use of Sparse Internal Validation Data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Multi-Hazard Risk Assessment (MHRA) critically depends on the availability, quality, and integration of spatial and temporal data. Such data can be obtained from diverse sources, including field mapping, surveys, remote sensing, sensor networks, online platforms, modelling, and artificial intelligence. Increasingly, the processing and analysis of these large datasets are supported by cloud computing platforms that enable rapid computation and sharing. Spatial data for MHRA can be grouped into reference data (base datasets for integration), hazard data (characterising the intensity and extent of hazardous events such as floods, earthquakes, and wildfires), exposure data (elements at risk such as population, buildings, and infrastructure), and vulnerability data (factors influencing susceptibility to hazard impacts). Establishing a robust data ecosystem is essential to combining and managing these datasets effectively. Frameworks such as the United Nations’ Integrated Geospatial Information Framework (IGIF) provide guidance; however, significant challenges remain, including inconsistent data availability, institutional barriers to data sharing, and high acquisition costs. Addressing these challenges is crucial to strengthening MHRA and supporting disaster risk reduction and resilience-building efforts.
evidence_items.title: Spatial Data for Multi-hazard Risk Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Purpose Financial technology (FinTech) is increasingly associated with digital transformation and broader sustainability-oriented economic objectives. Although previous studies have extensively examined technological and organizational determinants of FinTech adoption, less attention has been given to the entrepreneurial cognitive processes associated with strategic technology investment decisions. This study examines the relationship between Entrepreneurial Opportunity Evaluation (EOE) and Financial Technology Decisions (FTD) among Thai financial institutions and assesses the mediating roles of Risk Re-Categorization (RRC), Financing Constraints Alleviation (FCA), Information Asymmetry Reduction (IAR), and Operational Efficiency Incentives (OEI). Design/methodology/approach A quantitative survey was conducted among Chief Financial Officers (CFOs) of firms listed on the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET). Data were collected from 32 financial institutions and analyzed using Hayes’ PROCESS macro with bias corrected bootstrapping to examine the proposed mediation model. Findings The findings indicate that Entrepreneurial Opportunity Evaluation significantly influences Financial Technology Decisions both directly and indirectly. Risk Re Categorization, Financing Constraints Alleviation, and Information Asymmetry Reduction significantly mediate this relationship, whereas Operational Efficiency Incentives do not exhibit a significant mediating effect. Among the mediators, Financing Constraints Alleviation demonstrates the strongest indirect influence, suggesting that improved access to financial resources constitutes a primary strategic motivation for FinTech adoption within Thai financial institutions. Research limitations/implications The study is based on a relatively small sample of publicly listed financial institutions in Thailand, which may limit the generalizability of the findings.
evidence_items.title: Entrepreneurial opportunity evaluation for financial technology decision

evidence_items.summary: Nanophotonic sensing and light manipulation require control over optical spectra and localized electromagnetic enhancement. Finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations provide these responses, but repeated calculations limit exploration of multilayer geometries and material combinations. Artificial intelligence (AI) surrogates accelerate prediction; practical multilayer design also requires editable fabrication variables and spatially defined objectives. Here we present MetaField, a framework connecting fabrication-aware multilayer encoding, complex-field prediction, spectral readout, and constrained search. MetaField predicts spatially resolved complex electromagnetic fields and spectral responses, enabling the localization and quantification of local enhancement and joint geometry–material searches targeting specified spatial regions. The framework performs approximately one million candidate evaluations within hours, with microscopy and Raman measurements of coated nanopillars illustrating its application to practical device analysis. MetaField supports spatially targeted electromagnetic evaluation within a unified AI-assisted nanophotonic design workflow.
evidence_items.title: MetaField for Electromagnetic Evaluation and Design of Multilayer Nanophotonic Structures

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Fabricated and unresolvable references are an increasingly common problem in graduate theses. This study measures how widespread the problem is in a reproducible sample. 100 theses approved in 2026 were drawn at random (by thesis number, seed 20260920) from the Turkish Council of Higher Education (YÖK) National Thesis Center; the reference lists of 93 could be extracted reliably, and every reference in them was checked one by one against open scholarly databases: 14,888 references in total, from 59 different universities (50 master's, 26 doctoral, 17 specialisation theses). Results. 68% of references were verified in the relevant databases. 113 references carried a DOI that resolved to no publication at all, and 67 carried a DOI pointing to a publication other than the one described in the reference. Consequently 41 of the 93 theses examined contained at least one reference with a faulty identifier; by contrast, 27 theses contained no suspicious reference at all. Limitations. "Suspicious" is the output of an automated check and requires manual confirmation. Verification rates are lower for humanities theses that rely on Turkish-language books and archival material, because such sources are not present in open databases. The published dataset is anonymous: it contains neither thesis titles nor university names. Files. The report in Turkish and English (PDF), the anonymised per-thesis dataset (CSV) and the distribution figure (PNG). The living version of the study: kaynakcadogrula.com/tez-calismasi-2026 · referenceverify.com/thesis-study-2026 Türkçe özet. YÖK Ulusal Tez Merkezi'nde 2026 yılında onaylanmış tezler arasından rastgele seçilen 93 tezin tamamı denetlendi; 14.888 kaynak açık bilimsel veri tabanlarıyla tek tek karşılaştırıldı. 113 kaynakta DOI hiçbir yayına çözümlenmedi, 67 kaynakta DOI künyede belirtilenden başka bir yayına gitti; incelenen 93 tezin 41'inde en az bir kaynağın tanımlayıcısı hatalıydı.

evidence_items.summary: Predicting transcriptional responses across cellular contexts requires transferring both expression direction and differential-expression priority. We developed a compact numerical method that combines public perturbation summaries with a differential-expression kernel fitted to H1 CRISPRi training targets. The method centers an independent KOLF2.1J source on known training targets, transfers its response signs and magnitude ranks, and uses isotonic regression to render predicted expression means. We evaluated the frozen model retrospectively on the released public TEST100 of the 2025 Virtual Cell Challenge, using an external KOLF source released in 2026. The model achieved DES 0.371834, PDS 0.8614, and MAE 0.302206. With reconstructed historical anchors, its composite score was 0.341344, compared with the archived champion score of 0.340052, a difference of +0.001292. The comparison showed higher DES and lower PDS, with zero normalized MAE contributions for both methods. Source centering also improved development PDS across all three TRAIN folds and official VALIDATION. These results demonstrate a practical numerical approach to cross-context perturbation transfer and differential-expression ranking.
evidence_items.title: Centered cross-context perturbation transfer on the public 2025 Virtual Cell Challenge benchmark
