evidence_items.summary: Cancer patients with clinically similar tumors can exhibit substantial differences in disease progression and treatment response. Patient-specific gene regulatory networks (GRNs) may capture regulatory heterogeneity that is not represented by gene expression alone. However, strategies for clustering patients using these high-dimensional networks have not been systematically evaluated and it remains unclear whether clustering based directly on millions of patient-specific regulatory edge weights is computationally feasible at scale. We benchmarked feature-selection and clustering approaches for patient-specific GRNs inferred with PANDA and LIONESS across 9,778 primary tumor samples from 33 cancer types. We compared three data representations: gene expression, gene indegrees summarizing regulatory input to each gene, and complete networks of transcription factor-gene edge weights. Twenty combinations of four feature-selection methods and five clustering algorithms were evaluated using consensus clustering. Performance was assessed based on mean silhouette score, PAC score, concordance, computational time, and memory usage. Standard deviation-based feature selection combined with k-means clustering achieved the strongest overall performance for both GRN-derived representations, with overall scores of 0.997 for edge weights and 0.985 for indegrees, while remaining computationally efficient. Edge-weight- and indegree-derived clusters showed clinical, biological, and prognostic associations that were complementary to those obtained from gene expression. Together, these findings provide a practical framework for network-based cancer patient stratification and highlight the potential of GRN-derived features to reveal clinically relevant tumor heterogeneity beyond gene expression alone.
evidence_items.title: A Pan-Cancer Benchmark of Clustering Strategies for Patient-Specific Gene Regulatory Networks

evidence_items.summary: The development of abstractive text summarization for low-resource languages is constrained by the limited availability of high-quality datasets. Although Hausa is one of the most widely spoken languages in Africa, resources for developing and evaluating neural summarization models remain limited. This paper introduces Hausa Summarization (HAUSUMM) dataset, a curated dataset for Hausa news summarization comprising 11,482 article-summary pairs collected from four professional Hausa news outlets through an automated web-scraping pipeline. The reference summaries were derived from journalistic lead paragraphs and exhibit moderate phrase-level abstraction, as indicated by extractive-fragment analysis and n-gram novelty. To establish baseline performance, four summarization architectures, Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformer (BART), Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer (T5), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) with Attention, and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with Attention, were evaluated under controlled experimental conditions using Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (ROUGE) scores, BERT-based Semantic Similarity Score (BERTScore), and Summarization Consistency (SummaC). A human evaluation of the article-summary pairs was also conducted to assess relevance, factual consistency, coherence, fluency, conciseness, and abstractiveness. The results provide baseline evidence for Hausa abstractive summarization and make HAUSUMM available for further research on Hausa summarization.
evidence_items.title: A Hausa abstractive summarization dataset with baseline evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Modern generative models can produce visually plausible images while violating exact identity constraints. Evaluating such failures requires distinguishing violations of the requested identity from permissible variation in appearance. We introduce Low-Entropy Visual Identity (LEVI), which characterizes visual identities determined by compact facts and explicit rules. The low-entropy requirement concerns identity uncertainty, while appearance may remain diverse. We formulate identity fidelity in terms of the probability that a conditional image distribution assigns to the identities permitted by the prompt. Visual Identity Spaces (VIS) formalize this distinction by specifying admissible identity values and which different realizations express the same identity. Building on this formulation, we develop Verifiable Visual Grammar (VVG), a declarative language whose typed primitives and compositional constraints describe identity-bearing structures. Using this grammar, we build a benchmark for image generation. It assesses each output against the task's identity requirements, drawing evidence from the final pixels. The curated benchmark contains 1,375 tasks spanning 120 base identity spaces across six domains. Among ten evaluated model configurations, the highest whole-task pass rate is 58.69%. These results reveal a persistent gap between visually plausible images and faithful realization of their specified identities. Project page: https://maxiao0234.github.io/LEVI/.
evidence_items.title: LEVI: Benchmarking Visual Identity Fidelity with Verifiable Low-Entropy Constructs

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.
evidence_items.title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model

evidence_items.summary: Safe human--robot collaboration requires more than visual description: a monitor must determine whether the robot body is safely separated, already colliding with the scene or a person, or about to collide. We call this capability collision grounding: binding visual observations to robot body geometry, camera viewpoint, scene layout, human proximity, and temporal motion in order to infer present and imminent contact. We introduce TouchSafeBench, a physics-grounded benchmark for evaluating collision grounding in vision-language models (VLMs). Built in Habitat~3.0, TouchSafeBench contains 2,940 simulated indoor co-presence episodes across social navigation and social rearrangement, with synchronized multi-view RGB-D observations, top-down trajectory maps, calibrated camera metadata, and simulator-derived contact labels. We study two deployment-facing tasks: classifying the current safety state and warning about imminent collision before contact. Across three frontier or robotics-oriented VLMs and nine visual representations, current models remain far from reliable: the best average Macro-F1 stays below 50\%, explicit depth is not automatically transformed into robot-body collision evidence, and robot--scene contact is consistently harder than human-contact risk. TouchSafeBench reveals a central limitation of embodied VLMs: visual fluency does not imply physical accountability. Reliable robot safety monitors will need representations that explicitly bind viewpoint, robot morphology, metric geometry, and future collision. The benchmark is available at https://jun25336-bit.github.io/TouchSafeBench/ .
evidence_items.title: Probing Collision Grounding in Vision-Language Models for Safe Human-Robot Collaboration

evidence_items.summary: Existing text-to-video (T2V) evaluation benchmarks, such as VBench and EvalCrafter, predominantly contain either subject-centric prompts or static camera scenes, overlooking the importance of camera motion, essential for producing cinematic shots with realistic scenes. Due to this, the metrics developed in these works often produce incorrect results in the presence of camera motion. To fill this gap, we introduce DynamicEval, a benchmark comprising of systematically curated prompts that emphasize dynamic camera motion, paired with 45k human annotations on video pairs. DynamicEval evaluates two key dimensions of video quality: the consistency of the foreground subjects and the consistency of the background scene. To address the shortcomings of existing metrics under camera motion, we introduce two novel metrics: 1) Tracker-FG, which evaluates subject consistency by assessing the keypoint tracks of the subject. 2) Debiased Motion Smoothness, for background consistency, devoid from issues of occlusions/disocclusions arising from camera and foreground subject movements. Extensive experiments on the large-scale DynamicEval benchmark demonstrate that our proposed metrics achieve stronger correlations with human preferences at both the video level, and the model level with an increase of 0.32 in average Pearson Linear Correlation.
evidence_items.title: A Closer Look at Evaluation of Text-to-Video Models Under Camera Motion

evidence_items.summary: Self-improving agents built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for industrial fault diagnosis, but it is not known whether the experience such an agent accumulates over months of operation makes it more reliable or slowly corrupts it, least of all under edge-deployment constraints. We present LongHaul-Bench, a seed-reproducible synthetic industrial environment and protocol that follows an agent's knowledge state over about 1,000 sequential episodes with a quantized 3B-parameter model and a hard experience-memory budget. Across five independently generated worlds, experiential learning lifts exact accuracy over a frozen control by 3.8 points (complete rank separation; Holm-corrected p = .048). Plausibly corrupted feedback induces dose-dependent knowledge rot (-6.0 points at 40% corruption; -2.3, not significant, at 20%), whereas blatantly invalid feedback is inert. We explain these effects with a recall-precision decomposition computed on episode-matched pairs: memory adds about 9 points when a recall surfaces the correct precedent and removes about 20 points when it misleads, so memory helps only above a break-even recall precision of roughly 0.7. Plausible corruption leaves the cost of a misleading recall unchanged and instead lowers recall precision (0.81, 0.72, 0.65 at 0/20/40%); the precision drop alone accounts for the full loss at 20% and three-quarters of it at 40%. LLM-free manual-consistency gates recover the damage by restoring precision to 0.78, yet suppress two-thirds of memory's benefit when manuals are incomplete, and memory's value is an order of magnitude larger for a weaker 3B model family (+28 vs. +2.3 points). Generator, harness, run logs, and analysis scripts are released at https://github.com/vahit19/longhaul-bench.
evidence_items.title: LongHaul-Bench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Long-Horizon Reliability of Self-Improving LLM Agents Under Industrial Edge Constraints

evidence_items.summary: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
evidence_items.title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: NeuralSpeed: An Infrastructure-Level Approach to Efficient Large Language Model Inference Abstract The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) in enterprise applications, automated workflows, and multi-agent systems has increased the importance of inference efficiency, response latency, and infrastructure utilization. NeuralSpeed is an AI infrastructure technology designed to improve the efficiency of LLM-powered applications while maintaining compatibility with established deployment environments. The project investigates methods for improving inference efficiency in multi-interaction workloads, with an emphasis on operational performance, response consistency, and integration flexibility. The technology is designed to operate at the infrastructure level, reducing the need for changes to existing application architectures or underlying model parameters. Its development focuses on the following objectives: Inference efficiency: Improving the utilization of computational resources in supported workloads. Operational performance: Reducing unnecessary processing overhead where technically feasible. Integration flexibility: Supporting integration into existing AI application environments. Response integrity: Maintaining appropriate output structure and application-level compatibility. Deployment practicality: Evaluating performance under representative operational conditions. Initial evaluations indicate potential performance and efficiency benefits in selected workloads. Results depend on the workload, model, provider, configuration, and evaluation methodology. Further validation is required to establish generalizability across different deployment environments. Technical Scope NeuralSpeed is an infrastructure-oriented research and development project focused on the operational efficiency of LLM-based systems. This publication presents the project's general objectives, intended application domain, and high-level evaluation scope.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset collects the bibliographic records of printed intermezzos published in Italy between 1890 and 1960, as catalogued in OPAC SBN, the online union catalogue of the Italian National Library Service (https://opac.sbn.it). It supports the macro-level analysis of the article ‘Mapping the Intermezzo for Salon Orchestra in Early Twentieth-Century Italy: The Italian National Library System and the “Mo” Collection’, Fontes Artis Musicae (forthcoming). The corpus was built by searching OPAC SBN for the keyword intermezz? (the wildcard covers singular and plural) and the French equivalent entr’acte . The search was restricted to printed music published in Italy between 1890 and 1960. It was first run in April 2025 and updated in September 2026. The search returned 2,507 records. Each record was checked by hand and flagged for inclusion or exclusion. Excluded records are duplicates, pieces for solo piano, piano reductions of orchestral intermezzos, entries lacking any indication of an original orchestral version, pieces for non-orchestral small ensembles such as mandolin or wind quintets, and records no longer present in the catalogue. After filtering, 1,537 titles make up the working corpus of the study. Excluded records are kept in the file so that the selection can be checked and reused. Each record is also cross-referenced with two collections held at the Library of the Conservatorio ‘Giuseppe Verdi’ in Milan: the Mo collection (MO-ML), mapped by the MAPSEM project, and the MULEG collection. The MAPSEM data for the Mo collection are published separately by the MAPSEM project.   Related publication: Maria Sol Carona, ‘Mapping the Intermezzo for Salon Orchestra in Early Twentieth-Century Italy: The Italian National Library Service and the “Mo” Collection’, Fontes Artis Musicae (forthcoming).
evidence_items.title: MAPPING THE INTERMEZZO FOR SALON ORCHESTRA IN EARLY TWENTIETH-CENTURY ITALY: THE ITALIAN NATIONAL LIBRARY SYSTEM AND THE ETTORE 'MO' COLLECTION

evidence_items.summary: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
evidence_items.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video

evidence_items.summary: Agentic recommendation pursues shopper goals through sequences of context-dependent decisions. Developing and evaluating such policies requires faithful recommendation world models that capture both the interactive shopping environment and users' behavioral responses over long interactions. Existing resources rarely provide long-horizon, fine-grained real-user trajectories or support trajectory-level evaluation and offline validation against production A/B results. We introduce UserArena, a real-world e-commerce interactive benchmark containing 64,729 session trajectories from 11,010 users, spanning 566,102 items and 13 action types. UserArena pairs these trajectories with an interactive environment and supports offline validation against outcomes from a controlled production A/B test, enabling five-level evaluation from output validity and local decisions to sequential behavior, personalization, and outcomes. To improve simulator fidelity over these long-horizon interactions, we further propose On-Policy Trajectory Distillation (OPTD), which uses trajectory-level intent to provide dense teacher targets on student-generated rollouts. Experiments show that OPTD achieves the strongest overall fidelity among the evaluated simulators under UserArena's evaluation protocol and most closely reproduces the production policy effect in offline simulation.
evidence_items.title: UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Adverse event (AE) reporting systems are central to hospital safety monitoring, yet severity classification remains dependent on human review and may be subject to variability among reviewers. Large language models (LLMs) may support more consistent classification of safety reports. Objective To evaluate agreement between a large language model (LLM)-based classification system and adjudicated expert human classifications of adverse event (AE) severity, while characterizing variability in the human classification process. Methods We analyzed 286 adverse event reports from the institutional safety reporting system of a tertiary academic medical center. Two quality and safety experts independently classified each report according to an A–I severity scale aligned with the National Coordinating Council for Medication Error Reporting and Prevention (NCC MERP) framework; disagreements were adjudicated by a third senior reviewer to establish the final human classification. The same reports were processed by a prespecified LLM-based workflow whose configuration was fixed before evaluation, without training, fine-tuning, calibration, or prompt modification on the study dataset; when the workflow generated clarification questions, the recorded responses were used to produce a second classification. Exact agreement with the final human classification was treated as the primary descriptive agreement measure; one-category differences and larger discordances were considered separately. Results Initial exact agreement between the two human reviewers was 65.4% (187/286), with moderate inter-rater reliability (unweighted Cohen’s κ = 0.563; linear weighted κ = 0.740). The final LLM classification exactly matched the final human classification in 140 of 286 cases (49.0%); 125 (43.7%) differed by one category within the prespecified A–E near-match range, and 21 (7.3%) were larger discordances. Linear weighted Cohen’s κ was 0.728 (bootstrap 95% CI, 0.678–0.770).
evidence_items.title: Large language model–based classification of adverse event severity: agreement with final human classification in a single-center study

evidence_items.summary: Background: Mendelian randomization (MR) has been widely used to investigate causal relationships between exposures and outcomes. However, concerns have also been raised about the reporting quality of MR studies. STROBE-MR was developed as a reporting guideline for MR studies, but assessments of compliance with STROBE-MR in published MR studies remain limited and rely largely on manual review. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), it is now possible to automate STROBE-MR compliance assessment. Methods: We developed a pipeline using OpenAI's GPT-5-mini model for automated assessment of MR reporting quality. Model performance was evaluated on an annotated dataset of 46 eligible MR articles. We applied the pipeline to more than 13,000 MR articles published between 2005 and 2025 to assess compliance with the STROBE-MR guideline and to explore reporting patterns across STROBE-MR items, sections, and time periods. Complete compliance required reporting all applicable components of an item; a sensitivity analysis used a partial compliance criterion requiring at least one applicable component. Results: Our LLM-based pipeline agreed with the human consensus on 89.0\% of the STROBE-MR assessments. On average, 22 of 43 items (51.2\%) met the complete compliance criterion, with substantial variation in reporting rates across STROBE-MR items and sections. The least reported items were found in the "Methods", "Results", and "Other Information" sections. The number of reported items remained stable over time, with slight decreases after 2021. Sensitivity analysis showed that temporal trend patterns differed between complete and partial compliance, particularly in the Methods, Discussion and Other Information sections. Conclusions: This study demonstrates the potential of LLMs to automate reporting quality assessment in MR studies.
evidence_items.title: Reporting Quality of Mendelian Randomization Studies Based on STROBE‑MR: An Investigation Powered by Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Evaluating long-horizon robot manipulation policies is a high-throughput computing workload: one CALVIN-style campaign sweeps checkpoints, seeds and task sequences across many concurrent simulator workers, consuming tens of thousands of rollouts before any score is inspected. Evaluation-path correctness is therefore a workflow-validation concern in parallel evaluation: an adapter defect shared by workers can yield a well-formed table of zeros while scheduler and determinism checks pass. We report a CALVIN case study and use it to propose the Benchmark-Fidelity Diagnostic Protocol (BFDP): a cheap-first set of single-worker controls, run before a parallel sweep, that audits export horizon, teacher replay semantics and reset fidelity in a fixed order. On Composing Actions from Language and Vision (CALVIN) scene D with a vision-language-to-diffusion pipeline, BFDP separates three findings of three different kinds. For the two tasks with a measured effect onset, the fixed 8-step export ends before the observed onset, and across benchmark-critical tasks it retains only 12–16% of the mean teacher-episode length. This is a confirmed defect of the export path: across all 14 episodes, in a paired intervention with export horizon as the only changed factor, exact-reset teacher replay rises from 0/14 to 14/14. The symbolic path returns one canonical robot state for all 64 probed initial conditions; this is the benchmark’s documented neutral reset rather than a defect, and the resulting exact-versus-symbolic split measures the sensitivity of our open-loop teacher control to its start state. Exact continuous replay reaches 1/3 on an official three-subtask probe, which bounds what teacher replay can establish under the official chained protocol rather than indicating a further defect. The full set of controls is between 0.36 and 1.8% of the subtask-rollout workload of the campaign it precedes, depending on how far the policy gets before each official sequence terminates.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-path fidelity in parallel robot-policy evaluation: a CALVIN case study

organizations: School of Economics and Management, Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai 201306, China
evidence_items.summary: Maritime supply chains are exposed to pandemics, geopolitical conflict, extreme weather, congestion, equipment failure, and cyberattacks. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) supports resilience across maritime supply chains. The Web of Science Core Collection was searched on 26 August 2026 using intersecting AI, resilience, and maritime supply chain terms. The search yielded 336 English-language records. After temporal consistency checks, 328 publications from 2018–2026 formed the common corpus for bibliometric and systematic content analysis; seven earlier studies were consulted as intellectual foundations, and one record assigned to 2027 was excluded. CiteSpace mapping, structured coding, and conceptual synthesis produced four findings. First, publication output accelerated after 2023, and domain-informed coding of the keyword network identified seven connected themes spanning predictive intelligence, data infrastructure, operations, coordination, risk, and sustainability. Second, the literature concentrates on operational disruption, safety, and cyber risk and applies machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning mainly to vessel and port operations. Third, the synthesis suggests that AI contributes to resilience indirectly: model outputs must become organizational capabilities and enter strategies such as resource reallocation, substitution, and network reconfiguration before they can influence resistance, recovery, adaptation, or transformation. Fourth, much of the evidence remains based on single-site data, simulation, or routine operating conditions rather than on causal evaluation during actual disruptions. The review therefore proposes a theory-informed framework linking shocks, AI technologies, organizational capabilities, resilience strategies, outcomes, and boundary conditions.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Maritime Supply Chain Resilience: A Systematic Literature Review

evidence_items.summary: Cancer immunotherapy has fundamentally reshaped oncology by demonstrating that immune modulation can generate durable clinical responses in patients with advanced malignancies. However, the effectiveness of current immunotherapeutic approaches remains restricted by substantial interpatient variability, primary resistance, and acquired immune escape mechanisms. These limitations largely originate from the complexity of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), where malignant cells interact dynamically with heterogeneous immune populations, stromal components, metabolic networks, and molecular signaling pathways. Conventional biomarker approaches based on individual immune markers, such as PD-L1 expression or tumor mutational burden, provide incomplete predictions because they fail to capture the multidimensional nature of tumor immune interactions. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative approach capable of integrating large-scale biological datasets generated through genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, single-cell sequencing, and spatial omics technologies. Machine learning, deep learning, and emerging foundation models provide unprecedented opportunities to decode immune ecosystems, identify novel biomarkers, predict immunotherapy responsiveness, and accelerate the development of personalized cancer treatments. Recent advances demonstrate that AI-driven models can characterize immune cell states, reconstruct spatial immune architectures, and improve patient stratification for immune checkpoint inhibitors. This review discusses the evolving intersection between AI and cancer immunology, focusing on how computational approaches are transforming TIME analysis, biomarker discovery, and precision immunotherapy. We critically evaluate current challenges, including algorithmic bias, model interpretability, clinical validation, and regulatory implementation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Meets Cancer Immunology: Transforming Tumor Immune Microenvironment Analysis and Precision Immunotherapy

evidence_items.summary: The artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced Blockchain telehealth framework proposes a new architecture that addresses remote healthcare delivery challenges through AI and Blockchain technologies, making services secure, intelligent, and transparent. Traditional telehealth delivery models face significant data security, privacy, and trust concerns. This study addresses these issues by applying AI predictive analytics to assess service delivery risk among patient populations through patterns of telehealth utilization and accessibility across demographic, ethnic, and geographic cohorts. After collecting and preprocessing patient information from the Telehealth Services for Medicaid and CHIP Population dataset, a Gradient Boosting Machine model was developed, achieving 99.96 percent accuracy, 99.89 percent precision, 99.98 percent recall, and a 99.93 percent F1-score. The experimental evaluation showed promising performance, with very low gas consumption of about 22,500 units per transaction, a latency of 0.013 seconds, and a strong encryption throughput of 57.75 MB/s. These results confirm that the framework is scalable and highly efficient. Overall, the proposed framework would improve security, reliability, and interoperability in the telehealth ecosystem, supporting more robust, resilient, and patient-centered sustainable digital health initiatives.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-enhanced Blockchain Telehealth Systems: Pioneering Secure and Intelligent Remote Healthcare Delivery

evidence_items.summary: The Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI), mandatory under MARPOL Annex VI since January 2023, requires existing ships to demonstrate a design-efficiency level that a large share of the conventionally configured fleet cannot meet without intervention. The tools available to evaluate and plan for compliance, however, are limited: certification grade calculators are proprietary and opaque, while academic treatments tend to embed the computation within one-off scenario studies rather than provide a reusable, openly described instrument. This paper presents the development and preliminary verification of an open, single-file, offline capable web based tool for EEXI calculation and compliance screening. The tool implements the attained-EEXI method of IMO Resolution MEPC.333(76) for the twelve applicable ship types, computes the required EEXI and a quantitative compliance verdict, models the engine and shaft power-limitation (EPL/ShaPoLi) regime, and estimates, for non-compliant vessels, the limiting rating that would bring the attained index to the required value. This was developed under the V-Model methodology, which embeds verification and validation as a structural counterpart of each design stage. Software verification and external validation are reported separately. For verification, two independently written implementations of the governing equations agreed to machine precision (ε ≤ 10⁻¹² %) across a thirteen-vessel matrix of hypothetical test cases spanning ship types, sizes, regulatory boundaries, and the power-limitation regime, and the inverse solver converged to the intended root; this establishes internal consistency of the encoding, not regulatory correctness. For external evidence, the outputs are compared with a published worked example (≈0.2 % deviation) and found to be consistent with an established commercial calculator and with the peer-reviewed literature.
evidence_items.title: An Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) calculation and compliance screening tool: Development, verification, and benchmark comparison

evidence_items.summary: Healthcare organizations generate large and diverse datasets through electronic health records, medical imaging, laboratory systems, wearable devices, claims, genomic studies, and public-health surveillance. Big Data Analytics (BDA) can transform these data into insights that support clinical decision-making, early risk identification, personalized care, resource planning, and population-health management. However, the value of analytics depends on data quality, interoperability, privacy, security, fairness, interpretability, and integration into clinical workflows. This paper presents a literature-based review of the role of BDA in healthcare and proposes a conceptual, end-to-end framework that connects data acquisition, governance, integration, scalable processing, analytical modelling, clinical validation, and responsible deployment. The discussion synthesizes findings reported in published reviews and highlights practical barriers that may prevent promising analytical models from producing measurable improvements in care. Rather than reporting a new clinical experiment, the paper develops a structured framework and a set of implementation recommendations for healthcare institutions. It concludes that BDA should be treated as a sociotechnical capability—not merely a software installation—with continuous monitoring, human oversight, and patient-centred governance as essential conditions for safe and sustainable adoption
evidence_items.title: Harnessing Big Data Analytics In Healthcare

evidence_items.summary: When does one-step prediction support accurate accumulated state? We compare five small multilayer perceptron representation packages on a synthetic ledger controller with all output statuses represented in training. The primary endpoint is mean bounded six-balance error at horizon eight with equal family weights. The original frozen study fits 120 models over eight corpora and three paired seeds. Canonical sign-and-observed-amount prediction reaches 99.9975% mean in-distribution exactness but only 34.24% complete-state exactness at horizon eight. Its bounded accumulated-error contrast with canonical regression is -0.1450 (97.5% interval [-0.1562, -0.1337]); the conservation-package contrast is -0.0056 (97.5% interval [-0.0163, 0.0051]). The conservation package conserves every horizon-eight state while attaining 0.09% state exactness. An operational heuristic has lower numerical error but produces capacity-invalid states. The original twelve-fit support diagnostic fails its capacity gate in all six augmented fits. A separately frozen reviewer follow-up adds 192 fits addressing parameter budgets, loss weighting, an identical-head objective, a role-equivariant architecture and matched one-step versus four-step carried training. None of the 192 follow-up fits passes the balance-flip capacity-status gate. Mathematically equivalent flattened and teacher-forced controls exhibit different recorded outcomes, limiting isolated temporal interpretation. The new oracle-state and decoder diagnostics remain separate from the original primary evidence. Results are bounded to the specified generator and training packages; they establish neither a general failure of conservation methods nor real financial utility.
evidence_items.title: From Supported Transitions to Carried State a Controlled Ledger Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: This study, completed in 2026, evaluated the effectiveness of Project SMILE (Striving for Modernized and Interactive Learners’ Reading Proficiency Enhancer) in optimizing the reading skills of Grade 2 learners at San Ignacio Elementary School. Using a quantitative descriptive design with a pretest and posttest approach, the study involved 50 learners enrolled during School Years 2023–2024 and 2024–2025. Learners’ reading profiles were measured through the Comprehensive Rapid Literacy Assessment, while a survey questionnaire assessed the perceived effectiveness of the intervention. Frequency, percentage, weighted mean, McNemar–Bowker chi-square, and Pearson chi-square tests were used to analyze the data. Project SMILE provided contextualized, differentiated, technology-assisted, and interactive activities, including guided reading, vocabulary and sight-word exercises, literacy games, digital presentations, printed materials, and parent-teacher support. Findings showed substantial improvements in learners’ reading profiles. In School Year 2023–2024, 68% of the learners reached the At Grade Level category after the intervention, while 72% attained the At Grade Ready level in School Year 2024–2025. However, the pretest-posttest difference was not statistically significant in 2023–2024 ( p = .125) but was significant in 2024–2025 ( p = .024). Respondents perceived Project SMILE as effective in both school years, with overall means of 1.25 and 1.23, respectively. The relationship between perceived effectiveness and post-reading profile was significant in 2023–2024 ( p = .001) but not in 2024–2025 ( p = .143). Overall, the findings indicated that sustained, interactive, and learner-centered reading interventions supported improved reading proficiency, although statistical outcomes varied across implementation periods.
evidence_items.title: OPTIMIZING THE READING SKILLS OF LEARNERS  IN SAN IGNACIO ELEMENTARY SCHOOL THROUGH PROJECT SMILE  (Striving for Modernized and Interactive Learners Reading Proficiency Enhancer)

evidence_items.summary: We prove an improved lower bound of 0.097387436922 on the largest normalised Ingleton violation among four-variable almost-entropic vectors. Previously reported constructions reach approximately 0.0925, used as a rounded benchmark; the best published universal upper bound is 19/124. Conditional parity hashing combines local binary parity labels, one common linear hash, simultaneous conditional privacy amplification and joint conditioning. Applied to a 24-atom source of Matúš and Csirmaz, it subtracts a multiple of the uniform-matroid rank function U(3,4) from all fifteen entropy coordinates. The limiting signed score lies in [-0.097387436923, -0.097387436922], and finite-alphabet distributions with score below -0.09738 exist. This record contains the preprint PDF, manuscript sources, Lean proof sources, exact numerical checkers, build instructions and verification evidence. The main theorem, including the closed rate interval, score enclosure and finite-alphabet existence statement, was rebuilt and kernel-checked in Lean 4.35.0-rc2 with pinned Mathlib dependencies. The finite sampler and fixed-path optimality argument are written proofs rather than separate Lean declarations. Søren Riis is the creator and coordinator and directed the research. Astra/Codex and Claude contributed mathematical development, computation and verification; Claude contributed the Lean formalisation and adversarial review. The source construction is due to Matúš and Csirmaz; the paper gives full references to the earlier entropy-region and privacy-amplification work. AI checks do not constitute independent human peer review. Licences by component: the paper PDF, LaTeX sources and original figures are CC BY 4.0; Lean sources, Python checkers and build scripts are Apache-2.0. Third-party dependencies retain their own licences. Repository: https://github.com/SR123/conditional-parity-hashing
evidence_items.title: An almost-entropic Ingleton score below -0.09738: Conditional hashing of a binary parity structure

evidence_items.summary: The atmospheric characterization of Neptune-mass exoplanets serves as a crucial stepping stone toward understanding smaller, potentially habitable worlds. This study presents a comprehensive multi-resolution analysis of WASP-107b, a warm super-Neptune with an extended atmosphere ideal for transmission spectroscopy. Our purpose is to combine high-resolution (HR) ground-based observations (TNG/GIANO-B, GEMINI SOUTH/IGRINS) with low-resolution (LR) space-based data (HST/WFC3, JWST/NIRCam, JWST/ MIRI). Combining HR and LR spectroscopy provides complementary atmospheric constraints. HR resolves molecular absorption into unique line forests, disentangling overlapping spectral signatures between primary and secondary species. It probes the upper atmospheric layers and penetrates through clouds. LR preserves continuum information essential for measuring absolute abundances and probes lower atmospheric regions. This multi-resolution approach enables complete vertical atmospheric coverage while providing tighter constraints on molecular detections. We first validated previous LR studies, confirming strong spectral signatures of CO₂, CO, H₂O, and SO₂, along with weaker signatures of NH₃ and CH₄. For the HR analysis, we combined two transits from GIANO-B (0.95–2.45 μm) with three transits from IGRINS (1.45–2.45 μm), both providing R ≃ 48,000. After disentangling the planetary signal from telluric and stellar contamination using Principal Component Analysis, we applied cross-correlation techniques to assess whether LR-detected molecules are detectable at HR and to search for additional secondary species. Finally, the combined analysis is completed through a Bayesian atmospheric retrieval that simultaneously fits both datasets, leveraging their complementary capabilities to provide tighter constraints on atmospheric composition and structure. A fundamental observational challenge for this planetary class emerges from their orbital dynamics.
evidence_items.title: JOINT HIGH- AND LOW-RESOLUTION ANALYSIS OF WASP-107B'S ATMOSPHERE: COMBINED STRENGTHS AND INTRINSIC OBSERVATIONAL LIMITS (HoRS3S)

evidence_items.summary: Effective breastfeeding is crucial for infant and mother's health. Breastfeeding is a process of feeding an infant or young child with milk from mother's breasts. Babies have a suckling urge that enables them to take-in the milk, provided there is a good latch, a good position and milk supply. Adequate practical skills among postnatal mothers are essential to prevent the common breastfeeding difficulties. Despite the importance of correct breastfeeding technique, some postnatal mother may have inadequate practical skills. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of a demonstration method in improving breastfeeding practices among postnatal mothers. A pre-experimental study was conducted in Dharampur, Bareilly, U.P. The sample size taken was 30 postnatal mothers, sampling technique used was Non-Probability Purposive sampling technique. The data collection tool was (1) demographic data and (2) Self-structured Observation Checklist. The statistical analysis was done by SPSS software. The results showed that mean post-test score (21.47 ± 2.05) was higher than the mean pre-test score (11.27 ± 2.35). The mean difference was 10.20, which showed improvement in practice after demonstration. The calculated t-value (21.13) was higher than the table value (2.05), indicating a statistically significant improvement in breastfeeding practice after the intervention (p<0.05). The findings revealed that majority of mothers had poor practice regarding correct breastfeeding technique in pre-test. After the intervention, the level of practice was enhanced. In conclusion, the demonstration method proved to be a simple yet powerful tool in bridging the gap between knowledge and practice, ensuring that every mother is better equipped to nurture her child for a healthier future.
evidence_items.title: "A PRE-EXPERIMENTAL STUDY TO ASSESS THE EFFECTIVENESS OF DEMONSTRATION METHOD ON PRACTICE REGARDING BREASTFEEDING TECHNIQUE AMONG POSTNATAL MOTHERS AT DHARAMPUR, BAREILLY U.P."

evidence_items.summary: Abstract: Examples, stories, and cases connect abstract propositions with situations, yet their pedagogical usefulness does not establish their evidentiary adequacy. This conceptual article examines how case-based learning can support understanding, responsible judgment, and adaptive knowledge use without allowing memorable narratives to substitute for warranted inference. Building on an originating essay about the value of examples, the analysis integrates selected scholarship on case-based reasoning, worked examples, analogical comparison, narrative persuasion, epistemic cognition, and Cognitive Flexibility Theory. The methodology consists of purposive literature selection, conceptual differentiation, comparison of explanatory mechanisms, examination of boundary conditions, and development of an integrative instructional framework; it is neither a systematic review nor an empirical intervention study. The conceptual results distinguish five functions of cases: illustration, epistemic testing, engagement, relational comparison, and adaptive reconstruction. They also identify six connected design requirements: specifying instructional purpose, establishing provenance, selecting meaningful contrasts, scaffolding interpretation, assessing transfer, and recalibrating claims. Four propositions specify testable relationships among case diversity, comparative activity, evidentiary transparency, prior knowledge, and transfer performance. The discussion addresses the tension between simplifying instruction and preserving contextual complexity, the ethical consequences of narrative selection, and the evaluation of digital case libraries. The article argues that instructional value depends less on accumulating compelling stories than on coordinating the purposes, evidence, comparisons, and assessments through which learners encounter them.
evidence_items.title: The Case for Cases: From Compelling Stories to Responsible Reasoning and Adaptive Learning

evidence_items.summary: Dataset (MATLAB files) of holograms and reconstruction code used in: Piotr Arcab, Mikołaj Rogalski, Karolina Niedziela, Anna Chwastowicz, Emilia Wdowiak, Julia Dudek, Julianna Winnik, Paweł Matryba, Jolanta Mierzejewska, Małgorzata Lenarcik, Ewa Stępień, Piotr Zdańkowski, Grzegorz Szewczyk, Maciej Trusiak, “Deep-UV lensless holographic microscopy on visible CMOS sensors for low-dose centimeter-scale biochemical imaging”.   Contents The dataset contains multi-height in-line holograms of an amplitude USAF resolution target acquired at λ = 266 nm for pixel super-resolution (PSR) reconstruction. The following two files are provided:   Multi-height hologram stack Data USAF HPB.mat The file contains a three-dimensional array I with dimensions [2162, 3816, 20], where Y and X denote the spatial dimensions of an individual hologram, and the third dimension indexes 20 holograms acquired at different camera-to-sample distances. The holograms were normalized by dividing each original camera frame by its Gaussian-filtered version (σ = 60 pixels). The file also contains the corresponding acquisition and reconstruction parameters: dx — camera pixel size [µm]. lambda — illumination wavelength [µm]. zz — camera-to-sample distances in µm, corresponding to the 20 holograms. xi x, xi y — subpixel shifts in X and Y, expressed in pixels relative to the first hologram. All variables are stored in single-precision format.   MATLAB reconstruction code main.m A MATLAB script for multi-height pixel super-resolution (PSR) reconstruction with optional total variation (TV) denoising.   Experimental details Holograms were acquired in a lensless digital in-line holographic microscopy (LDIHM) setup operating in the deep-ultraviolet (DUV) spectral range.
evidence_items.title: Deep-UV lensless holographic microscopy on visible CMOS sensors for low-dose centimeter-scale biochemical imaging - Dataset

evidence_items.summary: This article examines pedagogical approaches and procedures for developing students’ creative competence through independent learning. It integrates acmeological, systemic, competence-based, person-centered, contextual, andragogical, holistic, and systems-activity perspectives to align individual learning trajectories with professional and creative growth. The proposed framework treats competence development as an ongoing process that cannot be captured adequately by a single final grade. It emphasizes recurrent observation of the frequency of nonstandard solutions, quality of project revisions, critical thinking, and students’ engagement in self-improvement. Three interrelated components structure the model: an axiological-motivational component supporting intrinsic motivation and personal goals, a divergent-cognitive component supporting creative problem solving, and a meta-reflective component supporting evaluation and revision. Implementation is organized into four stages: diagnosis of creative potential, design of differentiated learning pathways, practical-creative work supported by coaching and mentoring, and reflective assessment with iterative product refinement. The paper also identifies constraints noted during the research, including insufficient opportunities for creative activity, incompletely formed value orientations, and limited engagement in independent learning. Overall, the framework positions reflection and indicator-based monitoring as mechanisms for making students’ progress visible and informing further learning decisions. The proposed system is intended to support transparent, responsive, and sustained development of creative competence.
evidence_items.title: METHODS FOR DEVELOPING THE COMPONENTS OF STUDENTS' CREATIVE COMPETENCE IN INDEPENDENT LEARNING

evidence_items.summary: The ReROAD project aims to support the transformation of urban streets into multifunctional spaces that integrate ecological, social, and mobility functions through a biocentric, circular, and socially inclusive approach. Within this context, stakeholder engagement plays a central role in ensuring that streetscape transformation pathways are grounded in local needs, collaborative decision-making, and socio-ecological realities. This deliverable presents the Strategic Plan for Stakeholder Engagement and Governance of the three Urban Living Labs (ULLs) established in Bolzano, Coimbra, and Granada. The document provides the conceptual framework, methodological guidance, governance structure, and practical tools required to support participatory and co-creation processes throughout the project lifecycle. Building upon the quadruple helix model, the plan promotes collaboration among public administrations, academia, private sector actors, and civil society, fostering shared learning and collective ownership of urban transformation processes. The deliverable defines approaches for stakeholder identification and mapping, levels of participation, participatory methods, governance arrangements, communication strategies, and monitoring and evaluation procedures. It also outlines the phased engagement process that will guide the implementation of the ULLs and the co-development of streetscape transformation scenarios and masterplans.
evidence_items.title: Deliverable 2.1: Stakeholder Engagement Plan and Governance model for the three ULLs

evidence_items.summary: Description ----------- This dataset describes the 1,729 items (copies) of printed entertainment music held in the ‘Mo’ collection (shelfmarks MO-ML) of the library of the Conservatorio di Musica Giuseppe Verdi in Milan (RISM siglum I-Mc). The collection consists mainly of editions for orchestrina (small dance and light-music orchestra, with piano-conductor score and instrumental parts) published in Italy and abroad between the 1920s and the 1930s; 1,138 items (66 percent) date from 1927 to 1931. 1,229 items bear the ownership mark of Ettore Enrico Mo, a pianist based in the Genoa area. For each item the dataset records bibliographic and copy-specific data, the persons linked to the edition (composers, lyricists, arrangers, dedicatees, etc.), editorial series, material features (printed lyrics, alternative scorings, publishers’ catalogues, references to recordings), the films and musical works to which the edition is related, and the media or performance contexts it refers to. The collection was catalogued, digitised, and mapped within the research project MAPSEM (Mapping Printed Sources of Entertainment Music in Twentieth-Century Italy), University of Milan. Cataloguing follows the standards of the Italian national library service (Servizio Bibliotecario Nazionale, SBN) and is enriched with musicological and relational metadata in the MAPSEM database (https://mapsem.changes.unimi.it/). The dataset is the source of the figures discussed in: Maurizio Corbella, ‘The “Mo” Collection at the Milan Conservatory and the MAPSEM Database: Printed Popular Music in the Age of Mass Media’, Fontes Artis Musicae (forthcoming). The dataset is also used in Mattia Zanotti’s article in the same issue.

evidence_items.summary: Background: Postoperative pain after laparoscopic cholecystectomy is predominantly visceral in the first 24 hours and is conventionally managed with systemic analgesics that carry opioid-related adverse effects. Intraperitoneal instillation of a long-acting local anaesthetic targets visceral pain at its source. Aims and Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of intraperitoneal instillation of 0.5% bupivacaine combined with port-site infiltration in reducing postoperative pain and analgesic requirement after elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Materials and Methods: In this prospective randomized controlled trial, 120 adults (American Society of Anesthesiologists class I–II) undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy were randomized to receive 20 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine instilled intraperitoneally over the gallbladder bed, hepatic surface and subdiaphragmatic space together with 10 mL infiltrated at the port sites at the end of surgery (n=60), or standard care without local anaesthetic (n=60). Patients and outcome assessors were blinded to allocation. Pain was assessed on a visual analogue scale (VAS) at 6, 12 and 24 hours. Time to first rescue analgesia, 24-hour opioid, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and paracetamol consumption, adverse effects and satisfaction were recorded. Results: Mean VAS was lower in the bupivacaine group at 6 h (3.43±1.75 vs 6.88±0.99), 12 h (4.27±1.22 vs 7.82±1.46) and 24 h (3.80±0.40 vs 6.38±0.52; all p<0.001). Rescue analgesia was required by 15.0% versus 100% of patients (p<0.001), the time to first rescue analgesia among those who required it was longer (7.14±2.25 vs 1.70±0.74 h; p<0.001), and 24-hour opioid consumption was lower (5.83±16.19 vs 40.83±19.51 mg; p<0.001).
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Intraperitoneal Instillation Combined with Port-Site Infiltration of 0.5% Bupivacaine for Postoperative Pain Management in Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: A Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the input data, the model code, and the results of the study "Modeling Germany's hydrogen future: Insights into spatial distribution, imports, and policy alignment", published in Applied Energy 409 (2026) 127508, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2026.127508. The study uses version 4.0 of the open-source Global Energy System Model (GENeSYS-MOD) for Germany, disaggregated into its 16 federal states and two offshore regions (North Sea and Baltic Sea). The base year is 2018, and from 2025 the model runs in five-year steps up to 2050. Four scenarios are compared: Unconstrained, FEP, NoH2WasteHeat, and OffshoreH2. Four sensitivity analyses with 359 runs in total, all based on the Unconstrained scenario, vary the hydrogen import price in 2050 (56 runs, 0.5 to 10 EUR/kg) and the capital costs of electrolyzers, variable renewables, and hydrogen storage (101 runs each, scaling factors from 0.5 to 1.5). Files: Model.zip: GAMS code of GENeSYS-MOD as used in the study. Inputdata.zip: input workbook of the federal states and the offshore regions, and the GDX files the runs loaded, including the time series. Results.zip: full results of the four scenarios. Sensitivity runs.zip: result tables of the 359 sensitivity runs, with the script that summarizes them. sensitivity runs summary.csv: summary of the sensitivity runs with the results analyzed in the paper (domestic hydrogen production, hydrogen imports, and electrolyzer capacity by region and year). README.md: file structure, scenarios, sensitivity runs, the options of every run, and how to reproduce them.

evidence_items.summary: Introduction:  Disseminated herpes zoster (DHZ) is a severe complication of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection. This atypical form of herpes zoster occurs in 10–40% of immunocompromised individuals and may involve visceral organs. To date, studies reporting on DHZ remain limited. Therefore, this case report aims to describe the clinical manifestations of disseminated herpes zoster in a 64-year-old woman. Case Report:  A 64-year-old woman was referred from the intensive care unit (ICU) on August 12 th , 2026, due to progressively spreading vesicular lesions. Previously, on August 11 th , 2026, the patient had developed grouped vesicles on the left arm extending to the medial region of the left elbow, which were diagnosed as herpes zoster. The patient also had a history of malignancy, specifically high-grade diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), confirmed by immunohistochemical examination. Dermatological examination showed multiple grouped vesicles distributed along a dermatome on the left medial brachial region, as well as discrete vesicles in the thoracic region and contralateral brachial region. These findings supported the diagnosis of disseminated herpes zoster. The patient received oral acyclovir at a dose of 800 mg five times daily for seven days, along with topical therapy and 0.9% sodium chloride (NaCl) compresses applied to the exudative lesions. Conclusion: This case describes the clinical manifestations of disseminated herpes zoster in a 64-year-old woman. It highlights the diagnostic challenges posed by disseminated herpes zoster in immunocompromised patients. Identification of this condition requires careful evaluation of lesion morphology, distribution, and clinical progression.
evidence_items.title: Disseminated Herpes Zoster in an Elderly Woman: A Rare Clinical Manifestation

evidence_items.summary: Raw two-terminal voltage records of a hand-made transient hot-wire (THW) transducer (single platinum wire, 75 µm nominal diameter, 31.2 mm heated span) in distilled water. Two sessions were acquired in 2016: one in an ice–water bath (0.5–1.0 A) and one at room temperature (0.7–1.1 A), sampled every 2 ms for about 3.5 s. The source current was verified but not recorded, and the probe was positioned by hand. The dataset contains the original 2016 workbooks, the records extracted as CSV, and a Python script that reduces them to thermal conductivity with an automatic fitting-window selection and a power-normalised regression that accounts for the power rise at constant current; the script reproduces Table 1 of the associated article. The window-selection test is applied only below a noise limit derived from simulated records, which excludes the two lowest-current ice-bath records. Further Python scripts give the GUM/Monte Carlo uncertainty and reproduce the simulation that sets the noise limit. The dataset also includes the MATLAB code of the radial and axisymmetric thermofluid models and of the GUM/Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis, with precomputed results. Measured data and simulated results are kept in separate files and labelled as such. Associated article: A.G. Ostrogorsky, R. Ricciu, P.L.M. Buonomo, "Heat transfer around a single transient hot wire in water – Part I: Finite-wire bias of the measured conductivity", submitted to the International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer.

evidence_items.summary: In the semi-arid industrial basin of Bhilwara, Rajasthan, effluent discharge from textile wet-processing, dyeing, and finishing units contaminates ephemeral drainage channels and unconfined aquifers. This investigation quantifies toxic trace heavy metal concentrations (Cd, Cr, Pb) across the irrigation water–soil–crop continuum under a factorial field design () comparing an unamended groundwater control (C1–C4), vermicompost-amended organic management (OS1–OS4), and composite textile effluent irrigation (TS1–TS4) across four contrasting economic taxa: Wheatgrass (Triticum aestivum L.), Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum L.), Spinach (Spinacia oleracea L.), and Spearmint (Mentha spicata L.). Flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) following matrix-specific wet acid digestions revealed high contaminant loadings in composite textile wastewater: Pb (), Cr (), and Cd (), exceeding permissible national irrigation thresholds (CPCB/BIS) by -, -, and -fold, respectively. In harvested foliar biomass, trace metal bioaccumulation followed the species-dependent hierarchy: . Foliar lead levels in S. oleracea and M. spicata reached and dry weight, substantially exceeding the international WHO/FAO benchmark () and the national Indian FSSAI statutory threshold (). Cadmium exhibited high soil-to-plant transfer efficiency, yielding Bioaccumulation Factors () greater than unity () in all effluent-irrigated crops. In contrast, foliar metal levels in organic control treatments remained below the solid-phase Limit of Quantification for Cd () and within safe baselines for Pb and Cr. Human dietary risk assessments yielded Target Hazard Quotients () of for Pb and for Cd in S. oleracea, demonstrating serious non-carcinogenic health hazards through the food chain.

evidence_items.summary: An important underlying requirement for deep learning models is the availability of large datasets, however, in sciences such as chemistry and biology, generating experimental data of sufficient size represents a significant bottleneck. In this work, we probed the extent and nature of limited input data, characterize how several protein language models (pLMs) learned on suboptimal datasets, and investigated augmentation approaches to improve predictive model performance. We found that narrowing the distribution of protein-protein complexes in a limited dataset permits an order-of-magnitude decrease in training dataset size, if a model is only expected to generalize to in-distribution data. Similar results were found in active learning (AL), where both in- and out-of-distribution Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) showed a small but consistent increase upon augmentation of the training set with complexes produced by ESM-3, a generative pLM.
evidence_items.title: Building from the ground up: augmentation strategies to improve protein language model performance on protein sets

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can convert long documents into structured research variables. Auditability becomes difficult when evidence selection and model scoring are not stored. We study an inspectable scoring workflow that converts archived annual-report Evidence Packs into a five-dimension digital-transformation disclosure score. The design combines report selection, PDF-to-text normalization, bounded paragraph retrieval, and DeepSeek rubric scoring through a strict JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) interface; the original canonical prompt/run binding is not available. We evaluate three measurement questions and one secondary utility check: reproducible Evidence Pack construction, LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs, ordinal error/confusion diagnostics, and non-causal panel-use stress tests. The evaluation panel contains 476 firm-year observations from 64 firms for 2013–2024. The post-validation score shows high internal coherence for the additive rubric (Cronbach’s α = 0.893; first principal component explains 0.704 of standardized dimensional variance), substantial within-firm variation (mean within-firm standard deviation (SD) 2.901; 92.19% non-zero), and strong LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs (total-score Spearman 0.910, Pearson 0.921, mean absolute error (MAE) 1.273; dimension-level weighted kappa 0.665–0.823). Human–Human total-score reliability, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), is ICC(2,1) = 0.811. Baseline comparisons show lower error than frozen lexicon-count and firm-grouped term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) Ridge alternatives (MAE = 1.273 vs . 6.387 and 2.737). A 96-record rule-based retrieval audit shows high mean dimension coverage (0.936) but incomplete heuristic paragraph recall@30 (micro recall = 0.419); four audited zero-hit packs are false empty (4.17%). The main reliability claim is therefore bounded to shared archived evidence.
evidence_items.title: Auditable large language model scoring of annual-report evidence packs: human calibration, baselines, and reproducibility checks

evidence_items.summary: Human body contains endogenous metabolites, nutrients and xenobiotics chemicals. These chemicals can be detected in a biospecimen using high-resolution mass spectrometry instruments, yielding metabolomic and exposomic datasets. Mass spectral libraries are critical components of these workflows to annotate experimental data with chemical information. In this data descriptor, we report mass spectral libraries for human-relevant small molecules, that are generated using Google Gemini large-language model. Using an optimized chain-of-thought prompt and instructions, we have generated mass spectra for each compound at high/medium/low energy fragmentation level. Each spectrum was reported in the NIST MSP text format for easy to use by metabolomics software. These libraries cover 91,231 unique 2D structures from the Blood Exposome Database and the Metabolomics Workbench data repository. Technical validation was shown by comparing the Gemini-generated spectra against NIST 23 mass spectral database, which demonstrated 55% accuracy. LLMs represent a useful and accessible tool for expanding in-silico spectral libraries to annotate compounds in the HRMS data for human biospecimens and may accelerate the compound annotation in metabolomics and exposomics.
evidence_items.title: In-silico Tandem Mass Spectral Libraries for the Blood Exposome and Metabolomics Workbench Databases: Application of Gemini Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Against the backdrop of digital media iteration and the expansion of China’s animation industry, aesthetic discourse surrounding female animated characters demonstrates differentiated structural features across production eras and evaluation contexts. Existing research is constrained by fragmented indicator systems, single-modality data, and a lack of standardized frameworks to support long-term cross-era quantitative comparison. To address these gaps, this study constructs a three-tier aesthetic evaluation framework consisting of Beauty of Image, Beauty of Impression, and Beauty of Idea, and proposes a dual-perspective quantitative workflow integrating large language model-based text mining, multimodal visual feature extraction, and the entropy-weighted TOPSIS method. Based on 72 representative Chinese animated works, 851,217 raw user comments, and 261 standardized character images, this study analyzes the distribution of aesthetic dimensions in both narrative-comment and pure-visual scenarios respectively, and validates the methodological reliability from three aspects: inter-annotator agreement, human–machine consistency, and test-retest stability. Quantitative results reveal that the two contexts present divergent aesthetic weight structures: identity-related dimensions exhibit the highest discriminative salience in narrative scenarios, while visual morphological attributes dominate in pure-visual settings. Across production eras, the discriminative salience of static morphological dimensions shows a steady upward trend, whereas the differentiating power of traditional cultural aesthetic dimensions declines gradually. High-frequency aesthetic vocabulary presents identity-oriented structural features in narrative contexts and form-and-style-oriented features in pure-visual scenarios respectively, with an overall evolutionary trend shifting toward visual detail orientation over time.
evidence_items.title: A Long-Term Empirical Study of Aesthetic Differences in Female Characters of Chinese Animation: Quantitative Analysis Based on a Three-Tier Aesthetic Framework and Dual-Perspective Large Language Model Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Aim: To compare the quality, readability, and emergency referral performance of four major language models in answering post-septorhinoplasty patient questions in Turkish and English. Materials and Methods: A cross-sectional evaluation study comprised 31 questions: 20 routine postoperative and 11 emergency/red-flag scenarios. Each question was submitted once to ChatGPT, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, and Claude in Turkish and English within independent conversation windows. Two otolaryngologists independently evaluated the responses using the Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence tool. English responses were additionally assessed using Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, and Simple Measure of Gobbledygook indices. Emergency referral accuracy was evaluated separately. Results: Total quality scores differed significantly among models for Turkish routine postoperative questions (p<0.001, Kendall’s W=0.775) and for Turkish emergency/red-flag questions (p=0.009, W=0.350), whereas the corresponding overall differences for English questions were not statistically significant. Within-model language comparisons showed significant Turkish-English differences for routine questions across all four models, whereas no language-related differences were observed for emergency/red-flag questions. ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Claude provided appropriate emergency referrals in all 22 responses, whereas Gemini did so in 16 of 22 responses (72.7%). All models exceeded recommended readability thresholds for patient education materials. Conclusion: The performance of large language models in post-septorhinoplasty patient education varied by language context and question category. Although emergency referral performance was generally high, model-specific omissions occurred, and all models exceeded recommended readability thresholds. These findings support language-specific evaluation, simplification to improve readability, and expert review before clinical use.
evidence_items.title: Comparative evaluation of four large language models for postoperative patient education after septorhinoplasty: A bilingual cross-sectional study

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into financial services presents a transformative opportunity to advance sustainability goals, yet a systematic understanding of its current state and impact is essential. This review aims to synthesize existing literature on AI applications within the financial sector, emphasizing their role in promoting sustainability and environmental, social, and governance principles. The study screened 3507 articles published in ABS‐ranked journals between 2020 and 2025 on AI and sustainability, narrowing the sample to a core corpus of 181 articles for mixed‐method analysis combining bibliometric techniques with Python‐based data analytics. Synthesized findings reveal significant research prevalence across AI sub‐domains such as machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing within sustainable finance contexts. Although literature supports the potential of AI to act both as an enabler of financial inclusion and as a tool for environmental impact assessment, variations in study contexts suggest a need for further standardized research to fully quantify its long‐term efficacy.
evidence_items.title: Integrated Bibliometric and Computational Analysis of Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Finance

evidence_items.summary: Objective To conduct a systematic bibliometric review of artificial intelligence (AI)-based multimodal neuroimaging research in depression, mapping its evolution, collaborative networks, and intellectual foundations to guide future translation.Methods Records were retrieved from Web of Science Core Collection (search date: 1 September 2025) using terms for depression, neuroimaging modalities, and AI/machine learning (ML)/deep learning. English, peer-reviewed articles/reviews (2001–2025) were screened; 1,232 studies were retained after deduplication and filtering. Analyses included annual output trends, co-authorship networks (countries/institutions/authors), keyword co-occurrence clustering with burst detection, and co-citation/bibliographic coupling using VOSviewer (v1.6.20) and Bibliometrix (v4.5.1).Results Annual publications rose from <20/year to 202 in 2024; 2025 counts (n=173) reflect January–August only. The international network spans 42 countries/regions linked by 320 co-authorship ties (total link strength=1,228; density of approximately 0.37). USA, China, and the UK constitute the epistemic core, with expanding participation from India, Brazil, and Iran. Institutional and author overlays indicate a small-world, hierarchical organization (205 institutions; 10 collaboration communities; author network 168 researchers) characterized by a productive core and long tail. Six keyword clusters delineate a functional workflow: 1) biomarkers/phenotypes, 2) functional connectivity, 3) machine-learning/computational approaches, 4) multimodal/precision psychiatry, 5) diagnostic classification/algorithm development, and 6) structural imaging/comorbidity. Co-citation and coupling reveal a progression from early ML and connectivity foundations to deep/graph models, multimodal fusion, explainability, and treatment-oriented prediction.Conclusion AI-based multimodal neuroimaging in depression has evolved into a coherent, translationally focused field.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Multimodal Neuroimaging Research on Depression: A Bibliometric Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Physical rehabilitation helps patients recover from injury and regain functional independence, but social and structural determinants of health, including living conditions, income, and transportation, can limit access to in-person care. Telerehabilitation addresses many of these barriers by enabling patients to complete therapy at home while supporting remote monitoring. However, the lack of direct supervision may reduce patient engagement, motivation, and adherence to prescribed exercises. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer opportunities to develop adaptive, personalized rehabilitation systems that enhance the effectiveness of self-directed therapy. This scoping review examines current developments in AI-driven rehabilitation, focusing on the techniques used, evaluation methods employed, and user experiences reported across studies. By synthesizing recent research, the review identifies emerging trends, common challenges, and opportunities for future AI-enabled telerehabilitation systems that improve patient engagement and support long-term rehabilitation outcomes.
evidence_items.title: A Scoping Review on Rehabilitation Systems Adopting Artificial Intelligence to Boost Motivation
